#4942. Rio Tinto eyes a giant hot-brick battery to cut fossil fuel use

Rio Tinto wants to put Australia’s cheap midday electricity to work at its Yarwun alumina refinery – by storing it in hot bricks and using that heat battery to make steam after the sun sets.

The global mining giant and California-based Rondo Energy have started engineering and design work on a huge heat battery near Gladstone, Queensland. Rondo calls it Australia’s largest planned thermal energy storage project and says it would be a first for the alumina industry.

Alumina is a hard white powder made of aluminum and oxygen that’s used to make aluminum metal, sandpaper, and strong ceramics. Globally, aluminum sector refining accounts for roughly 175 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent annually.

It’s still at the study stage, but the potential payoff is substantial. Rio Tinto estimates the battery could supply around 5% of Yarwun’s steam needs and cut the refinery’s direct emissions by about 67,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide annually. It would replace some of the coal and natural gas used to generate steam.

Rondo’s heat battery uses electricity to heat refractory bricks, which can withstand high temperatures. The bricks hold that energy as heat, which is then used to produce steam for the refinery’s existing steam network.

That matters because industrial heat demand doesn’t stop when solar production drops. Rondo’s heat battery charges during hours when electricity is cheap and plentiful, then delivers heat continuously so factories can keep running.

The proposed Yarwun system would have 360 megawatt-hours (MWh) of thermal storage and deliver up to 30 megawatts MW of heat. The Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) lists its electrical charging capacity at 78 MW, allowing it to take in electricity faster than it releases the stored energy as heat.

For the refinery, another attraction is that the battery would feed into equipment it already uses. The study will assess whether that integration can deliver reliable high-pressure steam at a cost that makes sense.

“This project shows how Australia’s abundant energy can become a competitive advantage for industry,” said Dr. Kira Rundel, Rondo’s head of Australia. “Heat batteries allow manufacturers to use low-cost electricity to produce the reliable, round-the-clock heat their operations need.”

ARENA is providing an initial A$3.6 million for the engineering and design study. If the project moves ahead, the agency will provide up to A$38 million for deployment. There’s also a further A$33.3 million in contingency support.

Rio Tinto will match ARENA’s A$3.6 million study contribution. The company says its total investment over the project’s life is expected to exceed ARENA’s funding if deployment goes ahead.

“Reducing emissions from alumina refining is complex, particularly when it comes to generating the high-pressure steam needed for our operations,” said Rio Tinto Pacific Operations managing director Armando Torres.

“This study will help us determine whether thermal energy storage can provide a technically and economically viable alternative to fossil fuels for part of Yarwun’s steam requirements.”

The feasibility study is expected to take about 12 months.

#4939. How This New Orleans Hotel Went From Former Haunted House to Chic Destination

The Greek Revival mansion that sits at the corner of Prytania Street and Jackson Avenue in New Orleans’ Garden District wouldn’t know “dull” if it came up and rang the doorbell. The 1857 building’s first owner was a cotton merchant who died of yellow fever. Another owner was fatally struck by lightning. Fast-forward to the 21st century, when a Tina Turner impersonator bought the property and turned it into Magnolia Mansion, a B&B with suites with names like Vampire Lovers’ Lair and Moulin Rouge. A former professional boxer and local politics kingmaker took over, but things fell apart around the time of the FBI’s raid on the property.

Oh, and the estate is said to be haunted.

The Whit's moody mahogany-paneled library

Named in its B&B era by USA Today as one of the top places in the nation “to sleep with a ghost” the magisterial Harris-Maginnis House earned a spot on the city’s ghost-tour circuit with an ever-mounting pile of lore. According to a spooky tour-operator website, guests at the B&B reported various eerie happenings over the years, such as the sensation of somebody tucking them in at night or a presence watching them while they slept. There were also rumblings of mysterious footsteps and slamming doors. Ghosts or no ghosts, the new team taking over the place found gothic-coded wall murals and dark purple velvet hanging at every turn.

Who you gonna call to give an old haunt a new design vernacular? Gretchen Trauth, CEO of the New Orleans investment firm behind the New Orleans hotel, rang up Jensen Logan and Katie Leblanc Killen of Logan Killen, a local design firm known for infusing spaces with a beguiling mix of polish and patina. “The goal was a hotel where nobody can quite tell whether a designer has touched it,” says Logan.

Breakfast room with Pierre Frey wallpaper

“We wanted it to feel very storied, like it’s been someone’s house for a long time,” adds Killen. “There are these layered histories imbued in the furnishings and the art and accessories.”

Named for poet Walt Whitman, who spent three months in New Orleans around the time of the home’s construction, the designers have reimagined the property with a romantic, lived-in, and curio-studded aesthetic that tempts guests to sit down and stay awhile. Architect Seamus McGuire of New Orleans firm Cicada helped navigate historical codes and redraw the map to capture some of the glamour that had drained away in recent years. His blueprint called for converting a trio of bedrooms into lounges. A mahogany-paneled library is now a gallery of antique dog portraits and a repository of volumes from local independent Faulkner House Books. “It’s dark and moody, and where you might want to have a cocktail or a whiskey,” Logan says of the clubby room. Bookworms might also gravitate to the sunroom’s banquette seating, one of the wicker chairs on the wraparound porch, or the breakfast room, a delightfully matchy-matchy enclave covered in Pierre Frey Les Colonnes wallpaper and curtains.

The hardest room to get right, say the designers, was the main lounge. “It’s a giant space that isn’t always in use, and can be tricky to give life to when it’s empty,” says Killen. Intended to serve as a great room by day and an atmospheric cocktail bar come evening, the team layered in elements such as blue paint that reads ethereal by day and warm by night, a custom grid carpet to add a sense of tailoring to the expansive area, and an intimate salon-style wall of works by Louisiana artists, including Robert Moreland and Mallory Page.

Another tightrope walk was the second-floor bar. Landmark rules forbid faking history a space never had, so the team went openly Deco instead. “What we don’t want is to put a contemporary bar into a very historic property,” says McGuire. “You can’t give a false sense of history to a space.”

It will probably come as little surprise that the bedrooms resist uniformity. In addition to the classically designed units, a quartet of cozy garden rooms has low ceilings and glossy oxblood walls; three cabana rooms feel airy, with bamboo beds and high ceilings. “It’s not meant to feel like everything was changed by the same person at the same time,” Killen says of the narrative that she and Logan have introduced to the New Orleans hotel.

As for the supposed ghosts, nobody’s heard boo.

#4936. Redwood and Rivian set to expand their EV battery recycling partnership

Redwood Materials and Rivian are expanding their existing EV battery partnership, adding a fresh battery material recycling effort to the EV startup’s Normal, Illinois, vehicle factory and, potentially, other Rivian-owned sites.

As Tesla co-founder JB Straubel’s second act, Redwood Materials had a lot to live up to. Its plan to give used EV batteries a second life as energy storage for public- and private-sector buildings, construction sites, micro-grids, and (sigh) data centers makes plenty of sense, though. Enough sense, anyway, that Rivian decided to put the idea to work as it built out its R2 production line at the former Diamond-Star Mitsubishi plant in Normal. Back in April, the upstart EV brand signed on for 10 MWh worth of energy storage using repurposed Rivian battery packs – but that deal was just the beginning.

The new, expanded partnership between the two companies will see Redwood collect, sort, and recycle Rivian’s battery production scrap materials, putting them safely back into the manufacturing process with minimal waste and at a fraction of the cost of virgin material. What’s more, the new deal will see retired Rivian batteries put to use in other stationary energy projects before eventually recycling some 99% of those batteries’ critical materials (nickel, cobalt, copper, and lithium).

With the recent launch of what is sure to be the more popular, more affordable R2, that’s suddenly a much bigger deal than it might have been last year.

“Every Rivian battery pack that comes back to us is a potential source of domestic grid energy storage in addition to critical materials,” explains Straubel. “Redwood’s unique ability to integrate and redeploy Rivian batteries with our technology is an opportunity to enable fast, flexible, and more cost-efficient energy storage. As the demand and cost for energy keep rising, working with companies like Rivian is how we help meet these challenges.”

Rivian is the latest major EV brand to enter into a formal battery recycling partnership with Redwood, with the list of others including BMW, Ford, Toyota, and Volvo.

I’m into the oversized look and love that these sweats don’t fit too tight on the lower belly, since other popular sweatpants I’ve tested can emphasize that area too much. Wohlner also prefers them a bit bigger, as she can always roll down the waistband for a more snug fit around the hips.

“The only downside to these sweats is the length; the pants go well past my ankle, making them hard to wear outside,” says Juric. Nevertheless, Juric notes that they are great to lounge in at home. “Plus, I think sizing down would’ve solved the length problem,” she says.

Saladino describes these sweats as dreamy on the inside and cool on the outside. “These are the types of sweats you can wear outside of your house and look pulled together,” she says. She touts the retro stripe and the vintage-y broken-in look for giving them a more street style vibe. They come in tons of different colors to choose from, too. Although they’re a bit pricier, she says that Aviator Nation’s striking style and premium materials are worth the extra spend.

These sweats are more fitted around the waist, and get fuller as they go down the leg for a roomier, more comfortable fit. The interior is buttery soft and fuzzy for extra comfort. They do run small, so beware of that while shopping. Saladino went up to a large and says they’re the perfect fit. They also have a slight drop-crotch so you never have to worry about them riding up or being too tight around that area (IYKYK).

We’ve worn these in public and they look great with everyday fits like a wool coat, a chunky knit sweater, and paired with socks and sneakers.

Like Adanola, Aritzia has a great mix of loungewear, activewear, and streetwear. And these sweatpants won us over the second we tried them on. We love that they’re incredibly comfortable and very chic. The flared cut is super on-trend, and it doesn’t look overly tufted like most fleece sweatpants and jackets we’ve seen, making them pretty dressy, Wohlner says. I wear mine out and about all the time.

“The fabric is pillowy-soft and the fit is just the right amount of roomy,” says Juric. “Thanks to the fleece fabric, wearing these pants literally feels as if you took the coziness and warmth from your bed on the go.” Hint: if you want something that feels like a warm hug, these are your winners.

I personally like that these sweats have a skinny drawcord waistband, as I find it looks a bit more flattering if you want to wear them low-rise. They do fit on the looser side, so size down if you don’t want them to look too baggy.

Winter is on its way, which means we’ve been on the hunt for a pair of sweats to throw over our shorts or leggings to and from the gym, and we’ve officially found our favorite pair. We love layering the Andie Oversized Fleece Sweatpants over shorts when we run to and from the gym as the temp drops. They’re warm enough to protect from the cold, but lightweight enough to keep us from overheating and feeling sticky. And, of course, we throw them on during cozy days lounging at home.

We love these for layering as the fabric is unlined and relatively thin, so they don’t add much bulkiness to the clothes we have on underneath. Thanks to the blend of modal and spandex, they’re super breathable and stretchy, so they almost feel like nothing when you have them on. Plus, if you get a little sweaty, the fabric is moisture-wicking (big ups!).

However, if you’re looking for an ultra-warm pair of sweatpants to keep you cozy during long treks outdoors, you might be better off with another pair on this list (like the Aritzia Cozy Fleece Mega Flutter Sweatpant).

When I first felt these sweats in our fashion closet, I knew they were going to be the winner for the softest option on this list. And when I tried them on for the very first time, my suspicions were confirmed. In comparison to all the others, these feel like butter, but they’re pretty thin and lightweight, so they don’t feel too heavy. I usually find joggers to be less cozy than wide-leg sweatpants, but these fleece joggers feel like absolute heaven—I’ve even fallen asleep in these a few times.

And after Saladino tested them for a few weeks, she had similar things to say. “These are hands-down the softest sweatpants I have ever worn,” she says, adding that they feel like a giant hug. “They’re perfect for super-cold days where you want to snuggle on the couch.” We agree that these are more suitable for lounging than for errands or the gym, as they err on the casual side.

Saladino likes wearing these a bit bigger so they feel even more cozy, and the medium was perfect for that. They run a bit large, so opting for your normal size will give you that slightly oversized fit that we recommend. Even though they’re baggier, they don’t slide down at the waist. If you prefer your sweatpants to feel snug, opt for a size down.

Softness is a must when it comes to sweatpants, and stylist Jackie Schiavone says the right material is key.

We tested an array of styles and silhouettes for this guide, but Appelt says the most important thing to keep in mind while shopping for sweatpants is your body type:

Sweatpants are meant to be oversized, so you don’t have to worry as much about fit, as, say, jeans. But it’s important to make sure the pair you choose is still flattering. Look for a body-skimming fit that doesn’t cling too tightly to your thighs while sitting comfortably at your waist or hips. Also, pay attention to length. You don’t want your pant leg to drag on the ground while you walk, so consider options that come in petite, regular, and tall lengths, depending on your height.

I'm a style writer who's been testing activewear for years. I’ve covered everything from the best workout leggings to the best hoodies to the most comfortable slippers. #4933. This Shell-Shaped Villa Has Mediterranean Views and a Windswept Feel

When designer Federica Gosio talks about this project in Sardinia, she describes it as “an arch over the sea.” Gosio—who leads the firm bearing her name and is also a cofounder of Studio MILO—explains, “the truly unique aspect of this home is its ability to adapt to its surroundings, the sea, and nature.” Overlooking the bay of Porto Rafael, an area on the island’s northern coast famous for its remote location and its scenic beauty, the house resembles a seashell.

The villa looks like a white shell that has emerged from the sea to embrace the surrounding landscape .

There is no single guiding principle in Gosio’s design; instead, the shell-shaped villa embodies a capacity to adapt: “The aim is to give shape to ever-changing realities, integrating it with strength and grace into a larger context,” she says. It’s an approach that characterizes many of Gosio’s projects. This one springs from the rugged land where the home is located and pays homage to its setting through its design.

A custom-made bench follows the perimeter of the portico, wrapping around the space. At its center is a set of furnishings in wood and neutral-toned fabrics.

Working with Gosio, Alessandra Radaelli, the owner of this shell-shaped villa, created an organic, sculptural retreat. “We decided to honor the design legacy of Rafael Neville,” she says, referring to the founder of Porto Rafael. That meant “favoring a harmonious approach in which architecture blends with the landscape.”

Interior designer Federica Gosio on the terrace of this unique and intriguing villa.

The villa is characterized by curved lines and pure white surfaces that also have a textured quality. Rattan and straw accents add warmth to the space.

The home’s pointed arches, organic geometries, and natural materials were inspired by the earth and the sea. “The minimalist spaces were designed to embrace the sunlight, the wind, and the slow rhythm of island life,” Gosio explains. “It’s a project that interprets the Mediterranean in a contemporary way through a refined balance of memory, nature, and design.”

Every corner of this villa blends seamlessly with its surroundings: In this outdoor space, the shapes soften and the lines curve. At the center is a white rattan lounge set.

With its soft curves, the home feels as if it has been shaped by the winds that blow across Sardinia. During the winter, the Mistral here is powerful, sweeping across the island and reshaping the landscape. It looks almost as if the same process has taken place both inside and outside the villa. The reality is that this effect was a deliberate design choice to soften the edges of the villa and smooth out its different volumes.

This semicircular arch draws one’s gaze to the sea. In the foreground are two coffee tables by Mogg. In the background, on a terrace, rattan armchairs complement the organic curves of the seaside architecture.

Both inside and out, the villa is a whitewashed structure that follows the contours of the land. Gosio and her team have done away with straight lines, opting instead for a softer silhouette. The signature element of the home is undoubtedly the pointed arch, used for both the villa’s doors and its hallways. “The soft volumes, textured surfaces, and carefully placed rocks guide the visitor toward the entrance with its hand-brushed, iron arched door, custom-designed by Daniele Mingardo,” Gosio says.

The property’s garden is an idyllic green expanse leading down to the sea with junipers and various plants native to the Mediterranean framing the villa.

Interior designer Federica Gosio (on the left) and homeowner Alessandra Radaelli.

Surrounding the home are acres of land covered in lush Mediterranean vegetation leading down to the sea, with the route including green terraces and social spaces, including the panoramic pool and an outdoor kitchen. The feeling is that of an earthly Eden planted in a corner of Sardinia.

The organic arch reveals a living space featuring an Asawa sofa by Secolo, Dune side tables by Mogg, and a vintage rattan pendant lamp purchased on the Pamono website. The Paysage II rug is by Atelier Février, the blue ceramic Anfora Anulare vase is by Walter Usai, and the cups and saucers are by LR Ceramics.

The goal of respecting and celebrating the villa’s setting is also reflected in the colors and materials used throughout the home. “The white walls, the floors in Orosei marble with a bush hammered finish and ‘broken edges,’ and the organically shaped furnishings come together to create a measured and well-proportioned design, inspired by the neutral and warm tones of the soil here,” Gosio says.

Access to the kitchen is also through a large, sweeping arch. The custom oak cabinets are paired with WA ceramic tiles by Decoratori Bassanesi on the wall. The table, which resembles a sculpture, is the Luna Elíptica by La Nena.

Orosei stone, which is found on the coast of Sardinia, not only forms the floors but also the sinks (both indoor and outdoor), a clear example of how the island was integrated into the design. Rounding out the composition is a selection of vintage rattan pieces and sculptural creations by Pretziada, a creative design practice based in Sardinia, and its artisans. Nothing is left to chance and every element contributes to the home’s exquisite design and its appealing composition.

At the center of the dining area, which overlooks the outdoor space, is a Luna Elíptica table by La Nena. Next to it is a Lia Chair by Chiara Andreatti and Pierpaolo Mandis for Pretziada, a piece that is both handcrafted and contemporary, with roots in traditional Sardinian design. The Holden Linear Pendant Uplight is from Porta Romana. On the table are several ceramic pieces by LR Ceramics.

The infinity-edge pool blends seamlessly into the villa’s architecture. Alongside it is a sundeck surrounded by lush green foliage and aromatic plants.

The outdoor spaces in this villa are extensions of its interior. Wooden furnishings with a distinct nautical flair are set amid breathtaking green spaces with ocean views. On the table is a Mini Geen-A lamp by Kartell.

A custom outdoor kitchen with views of the sea. The sink is made of Orosei marble.

The pool has views of the sea and sunsets.

The primary bedroom, with its organic lines, overlooks the pool and, beyond it, the sea. The custom headboard is upholstered in a striped fabric. Next to it is a Holden Wall Light from Porta Romana.

In the guest room, the custom headboard sets the tone. Next to it is a pendant lamp with a rattan Braided Lampshade-Bottle by Ferm Living. Atop a stone nightstand, a vase by LR Ceramics.

In this bath, Totem tiles from the Nok collection by 41zero42 add texture to the wall. The sink is by Catalano, and the faucets are from the Sirius series by Rubinetterie Stella.

This bath, with its rich textural quality, is defined by the wall-mounted sink in Orosei stone paired with a Roma faucet set by Rubinetterie Stella.

This room evokes traditional Sardinian design with a custom headboard that’s a mosaic of shapes and neutral tones, upholstered in Zinc’s Cubilete Natural fabric. The Holden Wall Light is from Porta Romana, as is the Huxley Jordan Wall Light reading lamp.

#4930. The 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E gains a standard long-range battery and starts at $40,000

Ford opened orders for the 2027 Mustang Mach-E, which now offers a standard extended-range battery for under $40,000. A new Trail model is also joining the lineup.

Ford’s electric crossover SUV is back for another model year. The 2027 Mustang Mach-E drops the standard-range battery offered in the 2026 model and now comes standard with the larger 88 kWh battery.

The 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-e is available in five trims: Select, Premium, GT, Rally, and a new purpose-built Trail model.

The new 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Trail is available for a $2,295 package upgrade for the Select eAWD.

According to Ford, the new Trail package is designed to make “outdoor adventures across pavement, gravel, and dirt roads more accessible than ever.”

It features fine-tuned front and rear struts and springs, a Rally-shaped steering rack, 19-inch High Gloss Dark Carbonized Gray Wheels with as-cast graphics, and is 10 mm taller in the front and 15 mm taller in the rear than the base Mach-E.

The 2027 Mustang Mach-E Trail comes with standard 400W, 120V Pro Power Onboard. It’s available as an upgrade for other variants, including the Premium, GT, and Mustang Mach-E Rally.

Select and Premium models use the 88 kWh battery and are available with rear- or all-wheel-drive (eAWD) powertrains. The GT and Rally variants use the 91 kWh battery and are only sold as eAWD models.

Ford’s BlueCruise 1.5 comes standard on the GT and Rally and optional on Select with Tech Pack Lite and Premium with Premium Tech Pack models. The Trail requires the hardware selection at the time of ordering. It cannot be added later.

Meanwhile, the Ford Connectivity Package and Ford Security Package are standard across the entire 2027 lineup.

The base 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E Select RWD starts at $39,995. Including the $2,045 destination fee, prices start at $42,040.

While it is a bit more expensive than the 2026 model year, Ford no longer offers the standard-range battery. Ford said a new secondary front motor delivers the same performance as the previous unit but at a lower cost, enabling the lower-priced base RWD model with the extended-range battery.

We're at almost 80,000 miles in our Mach E GT and we'll drive it to 200,000+. It's a blast to drive and we've loved owning it. Feels as solid now as it did day 1.

Bought a set of summer tires at 43k miles. Other than that, and swapping between winter/summer tires, the maintenance cost has been $0.

We don't DC fast charge very often, so the slower L3 charging isn't a big deal for us - but does need improvement IMO.

Previously, the extended-range battery was available, starting at $45,345 on the 2026 Mustang Mach-E.

The extended-range (88 kWh) battery provides an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 320 miles in RWD models. Depending on the configuration, eAWD models offer 300 miles of range. The GT and Rally use the 91 kWh battery, providing 280 miles and 255 miles of range, respectively.

Ford will announce the final EPA-estimated driving range for the Trail model closer to when it goes on sale, expected in the first quarter of 2027.

#4929. Race Day Roundtable: Speed Stories From Runners Who Raced in On’s Cloudboom Strike 2

Three athletes competing at three different distances share their experiences—and satisfying finishes.

Running “fast” is objectively subjective. What’s fast for you could be slow for another runner and impossible for someone else. Fast can even mean something different for individual runners depending on factors like where they are in a training cycle, if they’re coming back from an injury, or the distance they’re running.

Some runners equate fast with a specific pace-per-mile. Brooklyn-based fashion designer Florence Canonoy, for example, said it’s about seeing her paces drop on her tracking app month after month. “I just run to feel good, and then I look at my watch and it’s like 8:15 [per mile], and I’m like, ‘oh, I’m getting fast,’” she told Runner’s World.

For others, like Mollie Kaplan from Florida, running fast has nothing to do with the time on her watch. “When I’m feeling confident and happy, I feel like that’s when I produce my fastest times—when I’m not putting as much pressure on myself,” she said.

And for Long Islander Chris Chung, fast is a feeling: “When I’m doing interval workouts, that’s what fast feels like to me,” he said. “It’s feeling the wind in your face, in your hair, and just feeling like you’re floating.”

Regardless of how you define it, most runners would agree that their footwear plays a role in just how fast they feel on a particular day, especially race day. Below, Canonoy, Kaplan, and Chung share what they each learned pursuing personal goals in different races—all while wearing the On Cloudboom Strike 2.

A content creator from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, who played lacrosse in college and has completed four marathons.

Distance raced in the Cloudboom Strike 2: marathon in Chicago

An industrial designer and content creator from Jericho, New York, who’s been running for 10 years and did his first marathon in 2025.

Distance raced in the Cloudboom Strike 2: half marathon in Vancouver, British Columbia

A fashion designer from Brooklyn, New York, who ran casually in high school and college and began taking running seriously this year.

Distance raced in the Cloudboom Strike 2: 5K in New York City

Race goal: Push herself while returning from a hip flexor injury

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and concision.

Co-created with athletes for marathons and half marathons, featuring our CloudTec Sphere™ cushioning system for a fast ride and Helion™ HF hyper foam for energy return.

Mollie: My first marathon in New York City in 2024 was my fastest. I’ve been wanting to PR since then. But going into Chicago, we had a yellow warning [weather alert] with less than ideal conditions. So I was a little frustrated because after training all summer in the heat, I was really excited to finally do a cooler marathon and was definitely prepared to PR. But I took the pressure off myself the last two weeks before the race. My goal was not to look at my watch. I just wanted to go based on feeling and not to freak myself out.

Chris: This was my first half marathon back from an injury, a stress fracture in my femur. I hadn’t run 13.1 miles in a year, so I was like, ‘I’m just going to let it come to me and see how I feel. Let me just keep it below 1:50.’

Florence: I was taking my last couple races easy, but this was the one where I actually felt really good. So I was like, ‘Okay, let me push for it.’ It was one of my first races where I really took it seriously.

Mollie: I felt pretty strong from the start and I knew that it was going to be a good day for me. I can usually tell from the first mile. And the Cloudboom Strike 2, they kind of give you speed without trying. So they propel you forward a little bit, which is really great.

Chris: I started at the front and got caught up in the wave of people going out quickly. Within the first quarter mile, I was running PR pace at 6:20s and thinking, ‘I’m definitely not holding this because I haven’t trained like this at all.’ So I pulled myself back. I knew there were some hills on the course, so I just kept it effort-based. The Cloudboom Strike 2 maintained its responsiveness even when slowing down a little bit. I really liked how the rocker didn’t feel too aggressive, so it didn’t feel like I had to stay up on my toes the entire race. But at the same time, the roll-off felt really smooth and helped me maintain my cadence fairly well. The upper was comfortable and didn’t feel overly tight. It had some leeway in it and it felt light and breathable.

Florence: At the beginning, I felt really good, so I started running really fast and the Cloudboom Strike 2 had really good return. I felt like I was bouncing the entire time and it was easy on my hips, so that was great. It was also pretty breathable, which helped because that day it was really, really hot out.

Mollie: I saw my mom, my sister, and my boyfriend four times throughout the course, and every time I saw them, I had a boost of energy right after. Mile 20 was a turning point for me because I was like, ‘I’m still feeling so good I could speed up at this point,’ which I’ve never felt before in a marathon. And then when I finally looked at my watch at mile 24, I knew I had two miles to go and was super close to PR. That’s when I started picking it up, and it was just such a great feeling.

Chris: There’s a section of the race where you run along the seawall in Vancouver; you’re literally running alongside the ocean. Since I train solo, sometimes I love no crowds and the quietness of everything. I turned off my headphones for a little bit and listened to my own footsteps, my own breathing, and just took in the view. And you have that wind coming off the ocean a little bit, and you just feel like you’re kind of cruising.

Florence: In the middle and at the end, obviously the people cheering really helped. But I also felt like my stride was really good, where I was just bouncing and flowing, and I didn’t feel any wobbliness or stiffness. I have shoes that are a little bit too stiff, and I feel something in my body or my hip, but Cloudboom Strike 2 was really good towards the end.

Mollie: [In the last third of the race], they felt really good and comfortable and my body was feeling good, which was a really good sign at that point in the race, but the shoes still felt super springy. And when I started to push the pace a little bit, it just felt like a natural stride.

Chris: Other racing shoes can be really firm and aggressive. With this shoe, I feel like that little extra cushion really felt good for where my fitness was. It’s a little deceiving because it can feel like your foot’s sinking in, but at the same time you’re getting that responsiveness back from it.

Florence: I think it did help in terms of the cushion. There was a big hill in Harlem, so that was a little bit difficult, but the shoe helped propel me forward.

Mollie: I PR’d by three minutes, which is super close when you really think about all the little things that could go differently. I’ve cried crossing the finish line of every single race I’ve run, especially those last 100 meters. I get so emotional thinking about what I just accomplished before even the PR. Just completing a marathon is something so incredible and something that I’m so proud of every time I do it. I think about all the time and work that I put in, the months leading up to it. It’s just a very overwhelming feeling as you’re crossing the finish line.

But when I saw my time, I kind of stopped a little bit because I was so excited and so happy. I’ll definitely be wearing Cloudboom Strike 2s again, and I would definitely recommend them to anyone who’s in the market for a new pair of shoes to race in.

Chris: I know I have the speed in me; I just didn’t know if I had that fitness in me. So it was a good feeling to finish in 1:37. I was happy that I was able to push my body a little more than I had in the past year.

Florence: I went into the race not looking at my watch. And when you start to hear the cowbells, that’s when I started feeling really good and I was like, ‘You know what? I’m almost done. I see the finish line right there, so might as well sprint it.’ So that’s what I did. It felt amazing. Everybody was cheering.

Mollie: Something I’m working on is having confidence in myself from the first mile rather than waiting till mile 13. I tend to second guess myself, especially on the start line. I can tell myself, ‘It's okay if you go a little slower, if you don’t hit your goal.’ And anyone else who’s training for a marathon or looking to achieve the same goal, I would say just have confidence in yourself. Enjoy the journey. Celebrate the little wins, especially in your training cycle.

Chris: To get back to that speed, I know I have to put in more speed workouts. And it’s about playing the long game, too. You can’t force it.

Florence: This race taught me the importance of relying on feeling and not paying too much attention to my watch. When I look at my watch a lot, I tend to run a bit slower. But when I just focus on myself, whatever’s playing in my earphones, and just feeling good and just doing it, I run faster. We have our goals, but rely on how you feel. I think the number one thing is just enjoy it.

A highpoint of On’s Cloudboom Strike 2 is the technology. CloudTec Sphere™ helps keeps your legs fresher for longer by absorbing more of the impact, so you can retain your speed deep into a marathon.

#4925. Tesla (TSLA) quietly cuts 2026 capex guidance to $20B

Tesla has lowered its 2026 capital spending forecast. In its Q3 10-Q, the company now says it expects capital expenditures “to be in excess of $20 billion in 2026,” down from the “more than $25 billion” it had guided since April.

The change was in the 10-Q Tesla filed Wednesday, not in the shareholder letter it released the same day. And it lands in a quarter where Tesla reported $1.53 billion of positive free cash flow, a number that depends a lot on timing.

Tesla started 2026 guiding to about $20 billion in capex. In April, it raised that to more than $25 billion, and in July, CFO Vaibhav Taneja reiterated the figure while Elon Musk called 2026 a “massive capex year.”

Now it’s back to “in excess of $20 billion.”

Tesla has spent $13.01 billion so far this year: $2.49 billion in Q1, $5.79 billion in Q2 and $4.73 billion in Q3. Hitting $25 billion would have required about $12 billion in Q4 alone, more than double its biggest quarter. The new floor only requires about $7 billion.

The 10-Q says 2026 spending is “driven by our SI initiatives, including investments in compute infrastructure and data centers,” along with factory ramps and Tesla’s fleet of “company-operated SI-enabled assets.”

There’s a catch in the cash numbers, though. Tesla had $3.67 billion of equipment and construction spending sitting in liabilities at the end of September, meaning it was booked but not yet paid. That’s up from $2.63 billion at the end of June and $1.63 billion a year ago. So Tesla’s actual spending is running ahead of the cash capex it reports.

Tesla reported $6.26 billion in operating cash flow and $1.53 billion in free cash flow after capex. Here’s how it got there:

Depreciation and stock compensation are normal add-backs. They reduce profit without using cash.

The working capital line is the one to watch. Without that $2.59 billion, Tesla’s free cash flow would have been about negative $1.06 billion.

Most of it came from bills Tesla hasn’t paid yet. Accounts payable rose $1.92 billion in the quarter and accrued liabilities rose $1.95 billion, including $722 million more in “accrued purchases,” goods Tesla received but hadn’t been invoiced for.

Another $1.26 billion came from deferred revenue, mostly energy storage. Tesla’s energy deferred revenue jumped to $3.30 billion from $2.31 billion. But not all of that is cash. Tesla disclosed that it billed SpaceX $588 million for Megapacks “that have not been delivered,” which SpaceX hadn’t paid at quarter-end. That amount sits in both deferred revenue and accounts receivable, which rose $565 million.

Those gains were partly offset by a $1.82 billion increase in prepaid expenses and other assets, and a small inventory build.

If you also count the $1.03 billion increase in unpaid capex, Tesla’s free cash flow on an “as spent” basis was closer to $500 million.

The capex cut comes a month after Tesla signed $30 billion of new credit facilities. The 10-Q details them: a $20 billion delayed-draw term loan maturing in 2029, and $10 billion of revolving credit replacing a $5 billion facility. Tesla hadn’t drawn on either at quarter-end, and it had $45.4 billion in cash and investments.

Rearranging the deck chairs ahead of the merger?

None of this is improper in today’s accounting standards, which we can argue are pretty awful. Paying suppliers later, collecting deposits, and booking capex when it’s incurred are all somewhat normal accounting, and Tesla disclosed them. But they explain why the “$1.5 billion of free cash flow” headline from Wednesday’s results says less about the business than it seems.

Underneath, Tesla made $718 million of operating income, less than its $1.17 billion in stock compensation, and before working capital, it burned cash. The timing items that helped this quarter will reverse when the invoices come due and the Megapacks ship.

The capex cut is the more interesting signal. Six months ago, Tesla was telling investors 2026 would be a massive spending year to build out AI compute, Optimus and Cybercab. Now it’s lowering the target in its 10-Q instead of the shareholder letter, while lining up $30 billion of debt. Either projects are slipping into 2027, or Tesla is spending less to protect its cash. Tesla should say which.

#4923. 10 Best Airbnbs in London With Brilliant Design (2026)

If London excels at anything, it’s lodgings with soul—from the silver-service glamour of Claridge’s to the shiny new scenes of At Sloane. But these days, it’s the city’s next generation of stays—creative, design-led rentals that might include a sweet stay tucked into a mews, a contemporary warehouse with exposed brick, or a period town house on a leafy street—that capture the true spirit of living like a local. In a place where nightly rates can soar well into four figures, claiming your own corner of the city feels more like the move. Here are the London Airbnbs where you can carry on like a local—homes that are made for sinking back into after a morning finding the best coffee or after a late night in Soho.

Perks: Sauna, sound system, fully-equipped kitchen, curated book selection, washer and dryer, centrally located near St. Pancras train station

Tucked away on a quiet corner in Islington, this three-story, Japanese-inspired stay is filled with wabi-sabi design moments you’ll want to steal for your own space. Guided by a minimal color palette, light-toned wood weaves cohesion throughout the interiors, which are outfitted with architectural details and decor accents. On cloudless days, sunlight bathes the upper levels, giving the wood flourishes a warm glow. The main living area trades a traditional sofa for tatami mats, where you can perform traditional tea ceremonies or simply enjoy a morning matcha. In the upstairs bedroom, camouflaged closets and drawers surround a grounded bed frame, while a freestanding tub placed right in front of the sleeping arrangements invites you for a relaxing soak.

The downstairs kitchen serves a helping of maximalism with its striking red marble center island and coordinating stove backsplash. Just steps away from the refrigerator, a hidden walk-in shower, sauna, and spare bathroom are discreetly tucked away. The owners describe this home as a “domestic gallery,” but its beauty doesn’t make it any less liveable. “Every detail is thoughtfully considered,” says shopping editor Audrey Lee. “A Space Residence reimagines mundane fixtures into modern design moments that make you feel like you’re living in art. Relaxing in the tub with a good book, enjoying a slow morning watching television in the kitchen, or taking a steam in the sauna are just a few ways the days will quickly pass in this lovely home away from home.” From $549 per night.

Perks: Garden views, elevator, luggage drop-off allowed, proximity to Notting Hill landmarks

The property has a cohesive design thread in its use of maximalism, though no two guest rooms look quite alike, providing a sense of unique eclecticism. King or double-sized mattresses in each of the minimally designed bedrooms provide the perfect respite after long days spent visiting London sights like the nearby Japanese-inspired Kyoto Garden and Fukushima Garden, as well as Hyde Park and Kensington Palace just a short walk east. From $721 per night.

Perks: Underfloor heating, gallery-like, architecturally designed

#4922. The 7 Best LED Face Masks for Men in 2026, According to Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

For battling blemishes and signs of aging, there are few better at-home tools.

AS SOMEONE RAISED on slasher horror movies, I was always going to gravitate towards LED face masks. But while their creepy Jason Voorhees-at-a-rave look is what initially grabbed my attention, the skincare benefits are what sold me on the products. LED face masks combine the firming power of anti-aging products, the depuffing of eye cream, the energizing boost of moisturizers, and the breakout-fighting strength of acne washes—making them one of the most versatile grooming tools out there.

LED masks use specific wavelengths of light to penetrate the skin and trigger cellular changes, according to dermatologist Dr. Hannah Kopelman, MD. This can include stimulating collagen production to reduce fine lines and support firmer skin, as well as treating acne-causing bacteria and calming inflammation to promote a clearer complexion. Some devices offer all of these benefits, while others are laser-focused (get it?) on just one or two. The key is to know what each is capable of and what service you’re looking for.

Dermatologist Dr. Brian Toy, MD, warns that the market is flooded with LED face masks that vary greatly in quality and effectiveness, so it’s best to start your search as informed as possible. To temper the confusion, I went ahead and used myself, along with fellow Men’s Health writers and editors, as guinea pigs. This way, you’ll know what works and what is merely an overpriced Halloween mask.

We gave Shark Beauty CryoGlow a 2025 Men’s Health Grooming Award barely a month after it was released; that’s how great this LED mask is. It offers four separate treatment options that cover anything you could possibly want out of an LED face mask. The Better Aging setting uses red and infrared light to reduce wrinkles and firm skin, while Skin Clearing mode combines blue, red, and infrared light to fight blemishes and even tone.

The Skin Sustain maintains glow with a quick mix of all three LED wavelengths, and Under-Eye Revive uses cryotherapy-inspired cooling to depuff and tighten the under-eye area. You can also use this under-eye cooling ability combined with the other treatments, which roll out in three increasing levels of chill. Each is between four and eight minutes, meaning you don’t need to dedicate much time to combat whatever issue you’re after. Under-Eye Revive, you can do up to 15 minutes if you’d like, but you only need five to be effective.

Dr. Peterson Pierre, MD, FAAD, likes that this device uses red, blue, and infrared lights so that you can get a full smorgasbord of benefits, like combating acne, fighting signs of aging, reducing inflammation, and helping regulate oil production. He also digs the cooling feature and three levels of intensity. I’ve been using my CryoGlow for months, and have seen a noticeable change in the smoothness and clearness of my skin, as well as reduced redness, using The Better Aging and Skin Clearing settings. But where I saw the most immediate results was with eye puffiness.

If I’m ever running on limited sleep or recovering from a night out, I pop the mask on, and after a few minutes of Under-Eye Revive mode, I look like I’ve actually slept. The light from this device doesn’t feel glaring when you’re wearing it, so I was able to successfully walk around and multitask during my treatments.

Plus, as someone who is generally sensitive to light, it also feels a lot less intense than other options on this list, and never inspired headaches of any kind. Not to mention, it’s easy to adjust and fits my face perfectly. I only have a few nitpicks. Given the expansive options and customizability of this mask, there is a handheld controller attached to it to help you navigate. While this makes firing up the device super easy and you don’t need to rely on an app, the controller can be a bit awkward to deal with while you’re in treatment.

You can’t put it in your pocket without accidentally changing the setting, so you have to hold it, which limits the multitasking you’re able to do. Also, the mask is bulkier than its main competition for best overall, the Dr. Dennis Gross Face Mask. But when you consider that the CryoGlow is also the cheapest full-face option on this list, it’s a fair trade-off.

Read More: Shark CryoGlow LED Face Mask Review

Dr. Kopelman has been recommending this LED mask to patients for years. She likes that it is FDA-cleared and offers both red and blue light; however, what she likes most about it is that it consistently delivers results. In terms of effectiveness, it’s equal to the CryoGlow. The only reason it just missed out on the top spot is that it’s over $100 more expensive and offers fewer additional treatments, like under-eye cooling. Beyond that, I find it just as successful at battling blemishes and signs of aging as the Shark Beauty.

Plus, the treatments are shorter, and you only need to wear this for three minutes a day to see results. Unlike many other options, like the CurrentBody or FAQ 202, which are made of more flexible material you can mold to your face, this design is rigid. While that may seem like a drawback, I loved it. Of all the LED masks on this list, I found Dr. Dennis Gross to be the sturdiest, and it fit my face perfectly. It’s slim, without feeling flimsy, and doesn’t weigh down my face like other similarly sturdy masks that tend to be a bit heavier, such as the Theraface Mask.

That being said, I possess an incredibly average build and face shape, so if you fall outside of those parameters, the singular and unadaptable design of this mask might not be as perfect a fit. Unlike the CryoGlow, it’s wireless when you’re using it and can be conveniently charged with any USB-C charger. This helps when traveling, though the solid design poses some challenges if you’re tight on storage space.

Similar to the Dr. Dennis Gross mask, this device is crafted with a hard, contoured shell; however, it’s far less slim. But it trades off this added bulkiness with its vibrating ability, which soothes facial tension and boosts blood flow around the eyes, brows, and scalp. It offers red, blue, and infrared light therapy to target acne, improve skin tone, and increase collagen production.

You can choose between three- or nine-minute treatment modes, though we found the longer sessions to be more effective. Sure, this mask can feel a bit heavy or bulky on the face, but the results are legit. In fact, some effects can be seen immediately, and they only increase from there. “After the very first time I used it, my skin felt softer, and my pores looked smaller,” says Senior Gear and Commerce Editor Ryan Brower.

“Over time, my skin tone looks more even, and my skin appears to be firmer, smoother, and less puffy.” He adds that the massaging, vibrating feature is relaxing, although it can feel ticklish or even chill-inducing at times. Since it sits close to your ears, it can also get a bit loud, especially when multitasking. Still, it’s really easy to switch between settings, turn on and off, and choose the massage style you want.

If you’re solely looking to combat puffiness, dark circles, and wrinkles, Lumin is the way to go. Sure, it looks straight out of an abandoned Lone Ranger In Space reboot, but there is no device better at rejuvenating the skin around the eyes than this mask. One tester saw noticeable improvements after days of use with this device. “I naturally have darker circles, but after consistent daily use for about a week, I saw a noticeable difference in the brightness and overall alertness of my eye area,” she says. The mask stays in place well, and the soft silicone padding makes it comfortable throughout each session.

Its adjustable design also ensures it fits all face shapes and sizes with ease. The same tester also saw a brighter tone and smoother skin after a couple of weeks of daily use. “While I don’t personally have under-eye wrinkles, I can see how this would be especially helpful for someone who does or for anyone who spends a lot of time in the sun,” she says. Not to mention, the Luminator is quick and easy to use—just three minutes a day with an auto timer.

Our testers found that this FAQ mask makes a strong impression right out of the box with its ultra-thin, flexible design, which feels more like a high-end sheet mask than a tech device. You’ll need to download the app to get the most out of this tool, however. There’s a single button on the mask, but without the app, we found that it was nearly impossible to remember its function or how to power it off.

Once the app is set up and the mask is synced, navigating the features becomes straightforward—just select your desired treatment and that’s it. Despite being covered in tiny LED lights, the mask feels surprisingly lightweight and comfortable. During the 15-minute session, testers reported no heat or noticeable sensation on the skin and even forgot it was on while doing other tasks, such as reading. The mask stays comfortably in place, even when looking down at a book or phone.

We also appreciated the included cleaning spray. For anyone with sensitive or breakout-prone skin, keeping the mask clean is essential, and the spray makes that simple. After each use, we cleaned and dried the mask before placing it in its pouch, which securely holds the device and makes storage hassle-free. One minor concern was the split at the bridge of the nose—designed for flexibility—which left one tester wondering if that area was receiving full treatment. Still, this didn’t deter them from continuing to use it.

Women’s Health fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says that the Qure Pro LED Mask has taken her nightly skincare regimen to the next level. After a month of use, she saw a dramatic difference in her skin’s appearance. She used to struggle with oily skin and frequent breakouts, but since regularly using the pink LED light setting, she says it has significantly reduced her sebum production. “I'm also approaching 30 (yikes), so I've been using the red LED light setting as well to help combat fine lines and reverse skin aging,” Accardi says.

Each session runs for three minutes and automatically shuts off when it’s done, so you never have to worry about timing it yourself. It’s perfect for anyone who wants results without the hassle. It’s one of the easiest, most low-maintenance skincare tools out there at a relatively low cost. That’s not to say $380 is cheap, but when it comes to legit, effective LED masks, you won’t find many other options under $400. It’s really just this and the CryoGlow.

If the more rigid masks, like CryoGlow, Qure, and Dr. Dennis Gross, are too bulky for you, but the FAQ is too small for your face, Currentbody will be your best option. This mask offers the most flexibility, with a silicone design that easily molds to the contours of any face, ensuring full coverage. This is as long as you tighten the straps. I’ve been lazy a few times with that, and it will start slipping off your face mid-treatment. In addition to the flexible fit, this mask feels super gentle on the face.

One of our testers used it only days after getting eye surgery with no issue. Didn’t bother her eyes one bit. That being said, it takes up to six hours for a full charge, which can be a bit annoying. This is the longest charge time on this list by a few hours, to be clear. I’m the type of person who pushes off charging a device until I absolutely have to, so this long charge time usually results in me skipping a day of treatment. But if you’re a better planner (to be fair, it’s a low bar compared to me), it’ll be less of an issue.

Depending on what skin issues or concerns you’re looking to address with your LED face mask, you’ll want to focus on which treatments it offers. This is driven by the color of light the device uses, which dictates its benefits. Some on this list offer multiple services, while others zero in on one. These are the common options:

While some are comfortable and allow for multitasking, there is no getting around the fact that you’re wearing a large light on your face. As a long-time migraine sufferer, having a light this close to my eyes for too long can be a trigger. But even if you’re perfectly fine with prolonged light exposure, you’ll want to know what the time commitment is before buying LED face masks, as they’re most effective when used regularly. Some are as long as 25 minutes, while others can be as short as three minutes. Keep in mind that not all are meant for everyday use; some (especially the ones with longer treatment lengths) may only need to be used a few times a week for max efficiency.

When shopping for an LED face mask, choosing a device that’s FDA-cleared is essential, says Dr. Kopelman. This ensures the product meets fundamental safety standards for consumer use. To be clear, however, FDA-cleared is not the same as FDA-approved—the latter involves extensive clinical trials and rigorous testing. Currently, no LED face masks on the market have achieved FDA approval.

For now, stick with FDA-cleared options, which means the device is proven to be as safe and effective as another legally marketed product. You might also see terms like FDA-registered or FDA-listed, but these simply indicate that the manufacturer has notified the FDA of the product's existence—there’s no review or evaluation involved. Because of that uncertainty, you won’t see any of those on this list.

There are a lot of LED face masks out there, and like any trendy tool, not all are created equal. So, before putting any to the test, I consulted with a panel of dermatologists on which devices were legit and which they recommend. They also advised me on what to look for in a quality LED face mask and the brands to focus on. Based on this intel, I, along with other Men’s Health writers and editors, put several masks to the test, evaluating each device’s effectiveness, ease of use, and how comfortable it was to wear.

As many LED face masks do not offer immediate results, we used each one for at least one month to ensure enough time was given to gain any possible benefits. Following this extensive research and testing, I landed on these seven LED face masks as the best for men in 2026.

The dermatologists I spoke to for this story were clear on this: you should be cleaning your device after every use. If you don’t, bacteria, oil, and product residue can build up on the surface and transfer back onto your skin, causing irritation or breakouts, which may ironically be what you were hoping to minimize by using an LED mask in the first place.

Dr. Kopelman says that LED masks should always be used on freshly cleansed, dry skin to ensure the light penetrates as effectively as possible. After the session, apply your serums and moisturizers—doing it beforehand can block the light and reduce its benefits. A hydrating serum like hyaluronic acid or a peptide-rich cream works especially well to complement the collagen boost from the treatment, Dr. Kopelman says.

According to Dr. Toy, be sure to skip any products that might react to light. For example, because retinol and vitamin C serums are photosensitizing, they’re an absolute no-go before any LED treatment. Dr. Chacon adds that reflective products like heavy oils or sunscreens should also be avoided during use as they can scatter the light and disrupt the device’s effectiveness.

#4919. Fortescue is using KUKA welding robots to handle 6 MW charging cables [video]

Humanoid robots aren’t ready to juice up the massive, 240-tonne electric haul trucks Fortescue is putting to work in Australia’s punishing Pilbara. Instead, the company is using specially modified and massively powerful automotive assembly-line robots from KUKA to wrangle the massive cables needed to deliver a mind-bending 6 MW of power to its trucks’ batteries.

While Chinese car brands capable of 2 MW “flash charging” are making headlines these days, Fortescue and Liebherr have been quietly working together to develop a 6MW charging system for their massive, ultra heavy-duty mining rigs since 2024 – but details about how the process actually works have been scarce.

Until now, that is. In a new video released by the company earlier this month, Fortescue explains how it delivers what amounts a controlled lightning bolt into the battery of its specially developed, 264 (short) ton Liebherr T264E electric haul truck. And, because the massive, liquid-cooled copper cables are too big, too heavy, and too dangerous for any human to handle, of course they’re using robots to get the job done.

“The challenge with a six megawatt charger is that nobody makes these, and therefore nobody makes a lot of the components, either,” says a Fortescue representative, in the video. “So, we’ve had to take systems and subsystems from different industries were using industrial robots that would normally be used for welding in a car factory.”

Fortescue was able to develop and refine its KUKA robots with help from a $10 million (AUD) grant from the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), which were earmarked to help the company develop a six megawatt (MW) fast charger test unit and support its ultimate goal of achieving true net zero operations by 2030.

“Leveraging our world-class capability in battery and charging solutions from motorsport, the fast chargers have been developed for the challenging conditions of the Pilbara,” explained Fortescue Zero’s then-Chief Executive Officer, Ellie Coates, when the grant was announced in 2024. “Equipped with robotic connection options, they will be able to power Fortescue’s future 240-tonne Liebherr T 264 battery electric trucks in just 30 minutes.”

No need to reinvent the wheel, Cruise ship and other large vessels have ben using shore power for years when docked. these typical range from 7 MW to 16 MW, just borrow their tech, a overhead crane to lift the cable and an operator to plug it on

The Liebherr T264E packs an impossibly large 3.2 MWh (3,200 kWh) battery pack – the equivalent capacity of about 40 road-going Tesla Model Y crossovers – to put that 30 minute spec into context. #4914. I’m a Run Coach. Here’s Why a Marathon Doesn't Have to Be Your Ultimate Running Goal

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

This time of year, after most fall marathons have ended and our feeds have seen weeks of people crossing finish lines at some of the biggest in the world in Berlin, Chicago, and New York, it’s really hard to avoid feeling like you should run a marathon. I personally have posted countless videos of myself on the internet saying, “I’m never doing this again,” and even I’m tempted to go back on my word every November.

To be fair, I love the marathon. I’ve run 12 of them. I’ve run them very, very fast. And I’ve run them very, very slow. My first one changed my life. It gave me the courage to move to New York City and try to figure out what to do after graduating college. Six months later, I became one of the first running influencers, and I’ve spent the 12 years since building a global community, Badass Lady Gang, to help thousands of women belong and redefine their relationship with strength, power, and what it means to be a runner.

But I also feel complicated feelings about the marathon. As a running coach, I’ve watched the same conversation happen online for over a decade. Somewhere along the way, newer runners are told, or quietly absorb, that the marathon is the ultimate finish line. Which makes sense, right? Our brains love order and hierarchy. When you think about what it means to progress in running, it feels logical: going faster and farther are straightforward ways to show you’ve improved. But that’s not how it works. The marathon isn’t the objective ultimate goal. Or always the most fun one. And, it’s definitely not something that every runner needs to chase.

Every year I watch too many runners struggle through the training not because they lack commitment or drive, but because they’re chasing a goal they didn’t fully want or that their life can’t accommodate right now. And honestly, it’s just a really hard distance to master! A fellow coach and pillar in the community, Peter Bromka, put it best: “The marathon owes you nothing.” I hate that he’s right. You spend months killing yourself (metaphorically) for one huge goal, and then anything can happen on the day. It’s too hot. You get hurt despite doing everything right. You have an off day and watch your goals fly out the window.

We’re in the largest running boom the sport has ever seen, and I think it’s largely because we’re lonely. One in five Americans said they always or often felt lonely or socially isolated in a 2018 study by the Kaiser Family Foundation. And the stakes are real: the U.S. Surgeon General has warned that loneliness carries health risks comparable to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day. Running is one of the few activities that genuinely makes a dent in the loneliness epidemic because pretty much anyone can be a runner (even though it is easier and more accessible for some more than others). You can be fast, slow, old, young—if you’re lacing up your sneakers and moving, you’re a runner. Come marathon season, we also hear stories of the incredible adaptive athletes who cross finish lines with a range of disabilities, too.

Basically, there’s a reason run clubs are hot right now. They give people a way to put their phones down and find a community. The more you show up, the more you see people of all shapes, sizes, ages, fitness levels, and backgrounds crushing distances you thought weren’t possible for someone like you. Before you know it, you’ve signed up for your first half marathon and everyone is asking when you’ll run a marathon. Once you get on that path, it’s hard to stop.

Loneliness isn’t the only thing fueling the boom. We’ve also lost the sense that we control our livelihoods, our schedules, our futures. A marathon is something you choose. It’s one place where you get to call the shots: you set the goal, decide how to train, and define what success looks like, even when curveballs come. It gives you back agency in a world that feels uncontrollable. And in an age when we produce our lives online, it looks great on a feed. It’s badass to train for a marathon, especially when you feel like you have nothing else exciting to share.

So yeah, it’s not just a feeling that everyone’s running a marathon lately. It’s real. Over 1.1 million people applied to London. Chicago saw a 12.2 percent jump in participation from 2023. New York jumped 15.1 percent in the same time period. Races sell out in hours. Getting a bib is almost as hard as finishing 26.2 miles. That’s not an accident.

I work in this industry, and I can tell you a lot of money is spent each year making you feel like you should run a marathon. Last year, New York Road Runners, the nonprofit behind the New York City Marathon, spent $3.8 million on advertising and promotion. And much of that content is built around one image: a runner crossing the finish line, arms overhead, tears in their eyes, sharing how they became the person they always dreamed of being. It works. It makes you believe transformation is possible, and it is. But the marathon industry has weaponized our deep desires to belong, to achieve, to become, and forced us on 26.2-mile slogs across our respective cities.

The result: This overwhelming pressure that everyone needs to get out there and run a marathon—and an exponentially growing number of sign-ups. Never in a million years did I think we’d get to a place where getting into a marathon was almost as hard as running it. But here we are.

I spent a decade being paid by the biggest brands in the world to promote the marathon. I built my business on being vulnerable online and sharing my own transformation through running. So believe me when I say: Not everyone needs to run a marathon.

Before I tell you why you don’t need to run a marathon, let me explain why I first decided to run one. It was never something I envisioned for myself. In my mind, “real” runners ran marathons. (Kooks, if I’m being honest.) Then, I graduated from college with a theater degree and had to start paying off my student loans. My community scattered. And I couldn’t run from the grief I’d suppressed after losing my brother my freshman year of college in a tragic accident.

On Thanksgiving morning in 2012, I started actually running from my problems. Running was brutal and wonderful in a way that left no room for my feelings. It demanded every ounce of attention just to keep putting one foot in front of the other or fall over and pray for a quick end.

I know. Dramatic. But I was the person who made the jokes about only running from the cops. Or a bear. I missed over 70 days of school my senior year ditching PE to avoid running. But desperate times! Running really did feel like a lifeline.

Running gave me structure and something to feel excited about. Becoming a runner gave me something to work toward and confidence when friends and family asked me what my plans were now that I graduated from college. Instead of saying, “I don’t know if I’ll ever work a day in my life doing the thing I love most,” I could say, “I’m training to run a marathon” and feel pride and purpose. They would look at me gobsmacked and impressed. “YOU! Running a marathon? WOAH!” Yeah, I’d think to myself beaming with pride. ME.

I went from couch to marathon in seven months. The running magazines I turned to for advice told me I shouldn’t do what I was doing. “You should run for at least a year,” “Going from couch to marathon shows you don’t respect the distance.” (Those were actual pieces of advice in articles I remember reading when I was training for my first marathon.) But I wasn’t running for a time goal. I felt like I was running for my life. I had to do it.

Training was horrible in the most fulfilling way. This was 2013 and learning to run was very different from what it is now. There were blogs written by former high school or collegiate runners or message boards with the type of runners who told you you didn’t belong if you loved to hate running like I did or ran slow. I didn’t know what I was doing. I made every single mistake you could possibly make training for and then running a marathon.

The biggest? I wasn’t ready. I grabbed a free plan from an app, ramped up my mileage way too fast, and got hurt almost immediately. I ran in shoes a size and a half too small. I didn’t know how to take energy gels (and ran the race with an absurd number of them sandwiched between my two sports bras). I wore nipple guards made for men, terrified my nipples would chafe.

And despite all the mistakes and missteps, running my first marathon saved my life. When I crossed that finish line, I immediately had this sense of if I could do that, there really isn’t anything I can’t figure out how to do.

I’ll never forget watching my first New York City Marathon from the sidelines the year I moved here. We were near the finish, at Columbus Circle, and I knew immediately that I had to run it the next year. I felt so proud to be one of the crazy people who had run a marathon, and so connected to what the runners were going through. There’s nothing like belonging to a group that has shared something so grueling and rewarding. And so, one marathon turned into two and before I knew it, I was a person who ran marathons for fun.

Coaching changed everything. I’ve watched a mom of three in her 40s break two and a half hours in the half marathon after years of believing she’d never be fast enough. I’ve watched countless women who’d been convinced they couldn’t be runners, because of what they endured in PE class, finally feel strong in their bodies while training to run a fast mile. I’ve watched women facing everything from depression to addiction pick up running as a tool and use it to get through the hardest stretch of their lives. And I realized the same joy, transformation, and belonging happen at every distance. There is no hierarchy.

But, it’s more than that. Oftentimes, when we talk about the marathon, we don’t grapple enough with the reasons it may be easier for some. Back in my 20s, the marathon was genuinely easier. Everything is easier in our 20s, even if it doesn’t feel like it at the time. We have bodies that recover much quicker, time that’s actually our own, and energy that feels endless.

I had all of that when I ran my first marathon at 24. I was braver, more naive (a gift!) and had no idea how to sit still in discomfort. I thought movement was the quickest way through, so I threw myself fully into crossing finish lines. (Funny enough, taking a break from marathons taught me what it means to sit in the hurt and actually do the work to heal.) That doesn’t mean that once you hit 30 or 40, your hopes of running a marathon are out the window, but it does mean that as you get older, you should be kinder to yourself if things feel hard or don’t look as shiny as they may seem online.

Which brings me to something we don’t say enough: a lot of the runners we look up to or love following on social media—the ones who are making us feel like we have to be a part of this—are often younger, and what we see is a story they’re producing. When you’re feeling inspired by a creator, or measuring your own training, chip times, or total races against theirs, remember who and what you’re comparing yourself to. This may be someone whose whole job is to run and work out, who has access to endless training and recovery resources, and who isn’t sharing the full story about their highs and lows. Social media literacy matters. Without it, we’re measuring ourselves against a bar that wasn’t built with us in mind.

When runners come to me and are deciding whether to throw their name into a marathon lottery or sign up, here’s what I tell them.

Not pressured. Not because you think it’s the logical next step. Compelled. That pull that screams, “I have to try this,” or “This matters to me more than anything else in the world.”

Marathon training is long and it beats you down, both physically and mentally. As a coach, my job is to help my runners uncover what’s really driving them: their real why. Because your why is the only thing that gets you out the door when you’re tired, sore, and regretting your entire decision. It’s the north star that keeps you lacing up on vacation, when your kid is sick, on a lunch break, before a wedding, on an 89-degree day, when every part of you is done. Without it, you’re just suffering for the sake of suffering.

It really is an unpaid (and expensive) part-time job. It requires hours of running and strength training every week—for months. It requires flexibility in your schedule and will leave you feeling exhausted, hangry, and spread thin for at least 16 to 20 weeks, depending on what your running looked like before you actually started marathon training.

And don’t even get me started on timing. You’re either training in the dead of winter where it’s freezing, dark, and icy when you wake up and get off work or in the summer when you’re juggling summer vacations and brutal heat.

How do you feel about running 15 miles around the Grand Canyon or in Italy? Is that doable? What about the weddings on your travel schedule? What do your weekends look like for the next four to five months? If you sign up for a marathon, they look like a whole bunch of staying in, waking up early to run double-digit miles, and obsessing over the forecast for this weekend’s long run.

Moms. Caretakers. People with busy, unpredictable lives.

I spend half my coaching time talking athletes off the ledge when life throws wrenches in their training and they feel like they’re failing. You end up traveling relentlessly for work and aren’t comfortable running in the dark in a city you don’t know. Or you hate the treadmill and have to do most of your training on one. Your kids get back-to-back-to-back sicknesses and you spend four weeks not able to run because you’re fighting off what they had. A parent ends up in the hospital. A partner gets a diagnosis no one saw coming. Extreme weather, which is becoming a new normal for many of us, makes training complicated or even inaccessible. The list goes on and on. Anything can and will happen during marathon training.

The question isn’t, “How bad do you want it?” That’s not how life works. No excuses? Tell that to a parent who doesn’t have reliable help. It's whether you have the time—real, uninterrupted time—to train the way you envision and the wiggle room to adjust to any and all of the above scenarios.

It’s about so much more than everyone posting their curated, perfect peak weeks.

Influencers know what to say to speak to whatever insecurities or fears you’re feeling. Or what to say to get just enough engagement, or outrage, to get our numbers higher. Running a marathon is big business and most of your favorite influencers are making a lot of money sharing their stories. Sometimes, it honestly feels like exploitation. Which is gross. But I wish more people understood that no one is sharing their actual lives.

The second you start filming yourself, whether you’re aware of it or not, you’re producing. You’re making choices that will resonate or earn engagement. So whether someone is sharing the highlight reel or highlighting everything that’s going wrong, remember that you will never know what’s actually happening.

Keep that in mind if you catch yourself comparing your undertrained or ordinary reality to someone else's seemingly perfect one. And keep it in mind when you relate to someone who says their training has been a train wreck too. I can tell you firsthand that making running interesting and entertaining is very, very hard.

If you struggle with perfectionism, marathon training may feel like you’re riding the struggle bus. But if you can train, show up imperfectly, and work with your perfectionism, look at social media with a grain of salt, and feel proud of what you could do, then you're in for an incredible ride.

I’m here to remind you that not everyone needs to run a marathon to transform their life, find belonging, or to have a great time being a part of something spectacular. I say this as someone who loves, reveres, and had her life changed because of the marathon: It really is just a distance. Real change doesn’t come from running 26.2 miles. It comes from specificity and intention and showing up for yourself, whatever that distance is.

There are so many other goals you can pursue with running that will give you the same result. Have you ever gone all in on a 5K? Or a 10K? Spent 16 weeks working to see how fast you can run a mile? Run the perimeter of your town with a group of friends? Can you train for a half marathon with a friend who has never done it before and be their cheerleader every step of the way? These aren’t less impressive goals. They’re your goals. And they hit just as hard.

Goals are empty without meaning. The marathon is a spectacle that feels like the ultimate test. But taking on the biggest, most difficult challenge in a sport isn't the only place where magic lives. You can find that same feeling in other distances, other challenges, and other ways of pushing yourself. The real work starts when you ask yourself one honest question: "Why does this goal matter to me?"

The marathon is an incredible accomplishment. But there is no hierarchy when it comes to distances and goals. It’s not a ladder. Just because you run a half doesn’t mean that you should run a marathon next. And, you can spend your whole life running and never even think of attempting a marathon.

You get to decide what fills your cup, what challenges you, and how you spend your time and energy. Only you have the power to choose what changes you.

So the next time FOMO creeps in and you feel like you’re missing out if you don’t run a marathon, remember this: You already have everything you need to change your life. You don't need 26.2 miles. You just need to show up for yourself.

Can you run a marathon? Yes. Should you? That’s entirely up to you.
