#4810. In 1828, serial killers sold their victims’ bodies to science

Published Oct 27, 2026 8:53 AM EDT

For as long as surgeons cut open living people to keep them alive, they have needed dead people to practice on. Today, donation programs keep medical schools supplied with the bodies they need to teach their students. But in 1820s Scotland, donating your body to science wasn’t legal yet. Nonetheless, one doctor found a way to get the bodies he needed. But it came at a terrible cost. This is the grisly story of the Anatomy Murders.

In the early 1800s, surgery was booming. A few decades earlier, Scottish surgeon John Hunter had helped bring a scientific view to Western medicine, transforming surgery with experimentation and careful observation. The Napoleonic Wars had boosted the demand for trained surgeons, Alun Evans, a retired epidemiologist at Queen’s University in Belfast, tells Popular Science.

One of the leading lights in this burgeoning field was Hunter’s compatriot Robert Knox, who ran an anatomy school in Edinburgh. But by 1827, Knox had hit a roadblock to his teaching ambitions. A change to regulations meant that dissection had become an important part of the medical curriculum. Knox’s school would require more than 400 bodies the following year. What made this such an overwhelming ask was that citizens had no legal way to donate their bodies to medical science. But where there’s a demand, supply will follow.

Edinburgh Medical School first opened in 1728, and for much of the next century, allegations of grave robbing linked to the school had been rife. Newly buried corpses would be exhumed and then presented at medical school doors by so-called “resurrectionists”.

The provenance of these bodies was unimportant to the corpse-strapped medical profession. But families, desperate to protect their loved ones, had taken extreme steps to stamp out the practice. Relatives would stay at their loved ones’ graveside for weeks, waiting for their bodies to lose their medical value. Factories produced devices like mort safes, heavy iron cages placed over newly dug graves. Knox had been forced to source his bodies from further away, even bringing some from across the Irish Sea.

Across the city, two other men also had a body problem. Irishman William Hare owned a lodging house with his wife near Edinburgh’s Grassmarket. One of his tenants was a fellow Irishman, William Burke. Burke and Hare became friends.

One day in early 1828, Hare discovered one of his tenants had died overnight. Even worse, the dead man still owed him rent. The pair came up with a plan to recoup the money, and they carried the corpse to Knox’s door. There, he paid them £7 and 10 shillings; more than a month’s wages.

Their eyes opened by greed, Burke and Hare hatched a plan to get Knox the bodies he desperately needed. Over the next 12 months, they brought him 16 fresh corpses. They had acquired each one by murdering their way through the poor of Edinburgh. They had lured the victims to Hare’s guesthouse, and then suffocated them in the night, lying on their chests to minimize any damage to their valuable bodies. The majority of their victims were women.

Burke and Hare’s rampage was only stopped in November 1828. A tenant at Hare’s guesthouse reported to the police that they had found a corpse under their bed. When the police raided the premises, they only found a single spot of blood where the body had been.

But under interrogation, Burke and his wife gave inconsistent accounts. Eventually, Burke, Hare, and their wives were all arrested.

Despite their equal guilt in their crimes, the two men had very different fates. Hare offered to confess everything to the authorities in exchange for his freedom. His evidence condemned Burke.

Two months later, Burke was hanged in front of a baying crowd. Ironically, his crimes meant that, under the Murder Act of 1752, he was not allowed a burial. His body was instead donated to the Edinburgh Medical School, where his skeleton is still on show today.

Hare disappeared after being freed. Evans says that research suggests he returned to Ireland, where some think he ended his days in Kilkeel Workhouse in County Down.

Knox faced graver consequences than Hare. He was never tried for his link to the murders, but his reputation was buried. He was forced out of a curatorial role at the Royal College of Surgeons and eventually moved to London. He was unable to secure another university teaching post, but continued to work as an anatomist at a hospital in the city.

Evans says the taint of the scandal went beyond Knox. “The Burke and Hare scandal really stymied medicine in Edinburgh considerably, and it explained the rising popularity of the Dublin schools and the Paris schools of medicine,” he says.

One fact that may have haunted Knox is that if he had avoided the lure of Burke and Hare’s corpses for just a few more years, he would have benefited from the Anatomy Act, passed in 1832, which gave surgeons the green light to procure any bodies from hospitals, prisons, or workhouses that had gone unclaimed for 48 hours. Voluntary donation was also legalized at the same time.

Instead, Knox became part of a black legend in Scotland’s history. Burke and Hare’s crimes have become an indelible part of Edinburgh’s grim past.

#4809. E-quipment highlight: the highest-rated mowers on Amazon are ELECTRIC (2026)

Despite decades of market dominance, it seems like the days of loud, finicky, gas-powered mowers may finally be behind us; and I say that because – for the second year in a row! – the highest-rated lawnmowers on Amazon won’t burn a drop of gas.

The latest round of dumb oil wars are ratcheting up fuel prices everywhere while, at the same time, state and local governments continue to tightening restrictions on noise and small-engine emissions. Combined, those things probably mean that your next lawn mower is more likely to plug in than fill up, whether you like it or not. The good news is that. in addition to being quieter, safer, and not poisoning the air you breathe while you walk behind them, electric laenmowers have come a long way in terms of power and performance in just a few years. So much so, in fact, that many of the highest-rated models on Amazon, emphatic period, are electric.

In putting this list together, we looked at the average star ratings of a number of lawn mowers on Amazon, focusing on products that had at least 2,000 reviews and a four-star average or higher, and found that (like last year) battery-electric units from EGO Power, Greenworks, and Worx were among the top-rated mowers, regardless of fuel type.

Here’s the rundown, in alphabetical order (by brand).

Over the past few years, the EGO POWER+ brand has staked a claim to being the gold standard for cordless lawn equipment, thanks to its high-voltage 56V battery platform and premium build quality. The brand’s 21″ POWER+ LM2112 push mower currently carries a 4.5-star average rating from more than 2,200 Amazon reviews and an “Overall Pick” designation.

That’s no surprise, given the LM2112’s 6 ft-lbs. of cutting torque (equivalent to a 150cc ICE), and up to 35 minutes of runtime (call it a suburban yard) from the included 56V 4.0 Ah li-ion battery, three-in-one mulching, bagging and side-discharge capability. It also starts at the push of a button, folds for compact storage and skips the exhaust, maintenance, and oil changes that come along with a comparable gas mower.

With an impressive 4.2-star rating after more than 12,000 verified reviews, the Greenworks 40V 16″ push mower is in rare company among mowers of any kind on Amazon. No surprise, given that the lightweight, cordless mower weighs just 37.5 lbs. and comes with a 4.0Ah battery and charger good for up to 40 minutes of runtime, making it ideal for homeowners with smaller yards who want to ditch gas without wrestling with a heavier machine.

The Greenpower’s 16″ cutting deck is designed for (if not limited to) compact lawns, with a five-position height adjustment and a two-in-one system offering you a choice of mulching (yes) or bagging (no) your lawn clippings.

For bigger, more demanding lawns, Greenworks offers a 4.4-star push mower with a 21″ steel cutting deck that’s powered by an 80V brushless motor and ships with a pair of 2.0 Ah batteries good for up to 40 minutes of runtime with both batteries. Three-in-one functionality for mulching, bagging, or side discharge is included, too, along with push-button starting, seven-position height adjustment, and a rapid charger that can get it back to work in about 30 minutes.

WORX’s 40V 17″ Power Share mower is another strong example of how electric lawn care can be both practical and affordable. The WG743 mates a pair of 20V, 4.0 Ah batteries to deliver 40V of power, and those same batteries work across the brand’s broader Power Share lineup of tools – a lineup that includes string trimmers, power drills, and more.

The WORX mower’s standout feature, though, is its “IntelliCut” technology that works a bit like traction control in your car, automatically increasing torque when the mower hits thicker grass (more traction) and backing off when it doesn’t need the extra power (when it detects wheelspin – or, in this case, cutting head spin). Factor in an intentionally lightweight design, seven-position cutting-height adjustment, and the de rigueur options for mulching or bagging, and you’ve got a versatile little mower for keeping a smaller lawn in shape.

#4808. Matt Damon and David Letterman Pop into The Gilded Age Just for Funzies

HBO’s period drama got a very modern surprise from two very recognizable faces.

IF YOU’RE NOT familiar with HBO’s The Gilded Age, it’s a pretty easy show to explain. Set in New York City during the titular era—the rapidly changing 1880s—the show is an exploration of the rich-people trials and tribulations of a new money family (led by Carrie Coon and Morgan “Train Daddy” Spector) and their neighbors, an old money family (led by Christine Baranski).

One of the show’s most important aspects is its production design, with intricately built sets and elaborately planned costumes helping to transport its viewers back nearly 150 years. Immersion is the name of the game.

With a setup like that, The Gilded Age is just about the last show where you’d expect to see a couple of our most recognizable modern stars walk directly across the screen—but that’s just what Matt Damon and David Letterman did, less than 10 minutes into the show’s season 4 premiere.

Damon, the Oscar-winning movie star who earlier this year led Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Netflix’s The Rip, and Letterman, the legendary talk show host, walked across the screen in full costume, saying nothing, in a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it moment.

As it turns out, according to a story published by Vulture, the whole thing was born from Letterman’s lifelong desire to make a surprise appearance in something as a background actor, something that began way back in 1977 when he saw a fellow comedian friend slyly appear in the background of a scene in Annie Hall.

In recent years, Letterman has apparently come close to shooting background scenes in Wes Anderson’s The Phoenician Scheme, the upcoming Michael B. Jordan-directed version of The Thomas Crown Affair, and Black Rabbit alongside Jason Bateman—but for one reason or another, none of them came to be.

Letterman filmed an upcoming episode of his current show, the Netflix interview series My Next Guest Needs No Introduction with David Letterman, with Damon, and discovered that Damon and Ben Affleck began their careers as background actors, and, for the sake of the bit, figured this would be the perfect opportunity to see his dream come to fruition. “We thought, Okay, this could be the perfect opportunity,” Next Guest showrunner Isabel Richardson explained to Vulture. “It’d be really fun for Dave to do this with Academy Award–winner Matt Damon, and it tied into his origin story really well.”

Damon, luckily, was into the idea too—and they made it happen. “It was a kind of hysterical moment when our production supervisor Leah Baker came up to me on set and was like, ‘Well, I have a kind of funny, interesting question: Would you like Dave Letterman and Matt Damon to be background on our set one day?’” Gilded Age showrunner Churchill said in the same Vulture story. “I just started laughing.”

Surprise appearances and cameos have long been a part of Damon’s playbook. Marvel fans certainly remember his brief appearances in movies like Deadpool 2 and Thor: Ragnarok, while fans of Damon’s frequent collaborator Steven Soderbergh’s movies won’t forget his surprise turns in movies like No Sudden Move and Che: Part Two. He even appeared in a very brief role in Ethan Coen’s Drive Away Dolls after working with Ethan and his brother Joel on the 2010 hit True Grit.

Perhaps Damon’s most memorable (and truly most random) cameo comes in the 2004 comedy Eurotrip, though. He appears early in the film as Donnie, the lead singer of an alt-rock band who sings a song about the affair he was apparently having with the main character’s girlfriend. “Scotty Doesn’t Know” is a pillar of both 2000s pop-punk and that era’s teen sex comedy movement, and Damon’s completely out-of-nowhere cameo is a huge reason why.

And, look, HBO seems to enjoy this kind of thing anyway. Just last month, we spotted the University of Nebraska’s head football coach Matt Rhule in the final episode of Lanterns. Does his appearance make sense in a show set in Nebraska? Sure. Did we ever expect to see Matt Rhule in an acclaimed, highly watched HBO drama set in a superhero world? No, we certainly did not.

It’s fun (and probably a bit trippy at first) to come to grips with seeing who you think you’re seeing. And if, somehow, you don’t know who either of those two are, you probably won’t notice at all and won’t think a thing. And isn’t that how all great cameos should go, really?

#4807. Can the BPC-157 ‘Wolverine’ Peptide Really Help With Pain and Recovery?

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Wellness seekers are increasingly turning to BPC-157, the wildly popular “Wolverine” peptide for injury recovery and pain relief, despite scant human evidence.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel voted in July to ease restrictions on it and several other peptides, recommending the injectable substances be made eligible for pharmacy compounding.

But before restrictions were eased, preliminary research suggests a rise in the use of the Wolverine peptide in recent years.

A September 2026 preprint analyzed more than 15 million medical records and identified 1,039 people with documented BPC-157 use.

The researchers found a roughly 33-fold increase in new users between 2020 and 2026.

The results, which were based on clinical records, have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

“The study found that BPC-157 use is largely hidden in clinical narrative rather than conventional prescription data,” said lead study author Venky Soundararajan, PhD, co-founder and Chief Scientific Officer of nference.

“The proportion of newly documented BPC-157 users who were male rose from 57% in 2020 to 70% in 2026, a statistically significant trend,” he told Healthline.

“The user population for BPC-157 peptide is increasingly male in proportion and increasingly younger with each passing year.”

BPC-157 is a synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide marketed and sold online for wellness.

Health claims about it and other peptides have spread on social media and in fitness circles and wellness communities, with high-profile advocates like Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. touting their benefits.

Proponents of BPC-157 claim the injectable peptide promotes injury recovery, pain relief, and tissue healing. Some advocates claim that “stacking” the Wolverine peptide, particularly with TB-500, may enhance its effects.

The “Wolverine” peptide got its nickname from claims that it facilitates rapid healing, echoing the regenerative abilities of the fictional X-Men character of the same name.

This promise of pain relief and recovery may be what gives the Wolverine peptide its appeal.

Soundararajan’s study found that nearly 33% of patients reported using BPC-157 for pain relief. By comparison, just 4% of patients reported using BPC-157 for performance enhancement.

Across the cohort of 1,039 patients, 27% reported improvements.

“Pain relief was the dominant reported benefit, documented in 183 patients,” Soundarajan said. “Wound or tissue healing was reported in 38 patients and functional return in 34 patients.”

“Part of BPC-157’s appeal appears to be to patients who remain symptomatic after chronic, complex or previously treated musculoskeletal problems, signaling a clear clinical unmet need,” he said.

Bert Mandelbaum, MD, a sports medicine specialist, orthopedic surgeon, and co-director of the Regenerative Orthobiologic Center at Cedars-Sinai Orthopaedics and Sports Medicine in Los Angeles, said that everyone experiences pain, but warned about the risks of using the Wolverine peptide to treat it.

“There is zero indication that BPC-157 has any efficacy for pain,” he told Healthline. “There’s zero evidence that shows that it’s good for clinical healing, and we don’t really understand the safety profile of it.”

Human evidence of the possible benefits and safety of the Wolverine peptide is limited.

A 2025 systematic review of current BPC-157 literature found that it was dominated by preclinical research and low-grade human evidence. The review authors said there was insufficient clinical safety data to determine the peptide’s risks.

A small 2021 retrospective study on the effects of injectable BPC-157 on knee pain suggests the peptide could help repair tissue and regrow cartilage. However, the study followed just 16 participants, lacked a control group, and did not assess impacts on function or quality of life.

An even smaller 2025 intravenous safety pilot on BPC-157 use involved 2 participants. While no adverse effects were reported during the short study, the researchers acknowledged that larger studies are needed to confirm safety.

The July 23–24 FDA advisory vote added BPC-157 to the Section 503A bulk drug substances list, allowing pharmacies to include it in compounded medications.

The FDA’s 8-6 vote, with one abstention, greenlit BPC-157 in both free-base and acetate forms.

The recommendation did not make BPC-157 an FDA-approved drug, nor is it a component of an approved product. The federal health agency has yet to make final regulatory decisions on peptides.

“RFK Jr. policies are hurting Americans,” Mandelbaum said.

“This decision is ridiculous. It’s another step in the wrong direction. There’s no basis for any of this stuff.”

The safety profile of the Wolverine peptide for use in humans is largely unknown.

As such, BPC-157 is banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency as an unapproved substance for athletes both in and out of competition.

The FDA notes that peptides like BPC-157 (free base) may be sensitive to product formulation, processing, environmental conditions, and impurities, which could degrade the products and reduce their effectiveness.

The health agency adds that it currently has limited safety information for how peptides like BPC-157 are administered.

Soundararajan explained that his study was unable to estimate the incidence or overall safety of BPC-157 because adverse events were captured retrospectively from routine clinical notes and are likely underreported.

“That said, the medical records examined contain both positive and negative patient experiences,” he said.

“Mood, sleep, skin, injection-site, and gastrointestinal symptoms are concrete safety outcomes among the few examined patient records with available evidence that deserve prospective measurement and discussions by healthcare providers with their patients who report using BPC-157.”

Some experts warn of short-term risks like infection at the injection site, but the long-term effects are not known.

“We don’t have publications of infections yet, but there are anecdotes of this,” Mandelbaum said.

“People are injecting their joints with this stuff, and you have no idea what it is. It’s not standardized. It’s not being regulated by the FDA, and I think people should recognize that. And although we haven’t proven it’s a safety hazard, we know it has no efficacy. So why do it? Why waste your money?”

Experts urge anyone considering BPC-157 or another peptide treatment to discuss it with their doctor first.

You might ask for evidence supporting its use, information on its quality, and whether there are alternatives with established safety and effectiveness profiles.

Mandelbaum noted there are many scientifically proven and safe alternatives to consider.

“We have spent the last 20 years developing an arsenal of biologics from PRP to bone marrow aspirate to adipose tissue to understanding glucosamine and hyaluronic acid,” he said. “We’ve done an amazing job at studying these things. We’re getting to the point where we are understanding the complexities of biologics. It’s exciting, and it’s impactful.”

Mandelbaum vehemently opposed the use of unapproved peptides like BPC-157.

He likened its rise in popularity to a “Ponzi scheme” promoted by “gym rats” and “internet influencers” who “leverage and exploit the gap between hope and knowledge.” Just because the FDA eased restrictions, he said, doesn’t make them any safer or more legitimate.

That said, any use of unapproved peptides should also be disclosed to a doctor.

“A short, open and empathetic clinical conversation can turn invisible consumer use of products like BPC-157 into useful clinical information that can critically help inform current and future care for such patients that ensure the best possible outcomes,” Soundararajan said.

BPC-157 should not be combined with other experimental peptides until research determines the potential for adverse reactions or events. Long-term use of BPC-157 and other peptides marketed for wellness is not advised.

#4806. A three-legged cougar named Crimson is thriving in Arkansas

Published Oct 27, 2026 11:06 AM EDT

At first, the video seems to feature an empty habitat. There’s a crate filled with hay, platforms of various heights, and a ball hanging from a rope. Then a furry head peaks out from behind the crate. A few seconds later, a large wild cat bounds into view, rushing toward whoever is holding the camera. The young mountain lion (Puma concolor) appears so happy to see the videographer that you almost can’t tell he has only three legs.

“Crimson was just three weeks old when National Park Service biologists and then California Department of Fish and Wildlife determined he had been abandoned,” Emily McCormack, an animal curator at Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge in northwest Arkansas, tells Popular Science. “Using GPS collar data from his mother and camera monitoring, it was confirmed that she had moved to a different den site and was no longer returning to care for him.”

As if the situation could get any worse for the young mountain lion, he also had an injury to his hind foot. Without treatment, the injury ultimately could have killed him. He was rescued and transported to the Los Angeles Zoo, where he received acute veterinary care. Then he was taken to Oakland Zoo by Flying Tails animal air ambulance service. The Oakland Zoo veterinary hospital team eventually amputated the injured leg.

Thankfully, Crimson made an exceptional recovery, but he was too young to be considered for rehabilitation and release. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife decided Crimson would live permanently at Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge, a safe haven accredited by the Global Federation of Animal Sanctuaries. And now it seems safe to say that Crimson has settled well into his forever home.

“He is thriving in his new habitat at our sanctuary. We chose a long habitat enclosure with relatively flat ground, where he can explore but also has the ability to fully run a good distance,” says McCormack. “Crimson loves his neighbors, especially a female lion named Lucy. He loves his meal times and can be heard chirping all day to the staff, interns, and guests.”

Mountain lions, also known as cougars or pumas, are native to parts of the Americas and represent the world’s most wide-ranging cat species.

#4805. Battery electric, solar-powered reefer units reach their first customers

The first regular production solar-powered electric trailer refrigeration unit (TRU) in Australia has hit the road with a real customer. Family-owned transport giant Wickham Freight Lines took delivery of the revolutionary reefer just this week.

Refrigerated trailers (reefers) are critical for hauling fresh food and flowers from the farm to your local market — the problem is that they pollute like crazy, powered by high sulfur, red-dye diesel-powered generators that run around the clock, even if the truck pulling them is fully electric. That constant diesel burn spews CO₂ and NOx into industrial and residential areas alike, and contributes significantly to fleets’ carbon emissions and noise pollution at a time when a number of municipalities are moving to regulate both.

It is, as they say, “a real problem,” but Sunswap Endurance cracked it with a solar-powered reefer that can keep food and pharmaceuticals cold in transit without burning a drop of diesel fuel – and now, they have real customers.

One of Australia’s largest privately owned trucking companies, Wickham Freight Lines decided to purchase the Sunswap Endurance solar trailer units following an initial trial, running from Sydney to Brisbane and back this past summer on a route covering a total of 1,670 km (~1,040 miles) over more than 30 hours of driving.

After Wickham’s drivers finished the round trip with over 65% of the battery’s capacity still left, the purchase was a no-brainer.

“I put the Sunswap Endurance into the fleet and told the team to stretch it — treat it as a normal unit,” explains Graham Keogh, director at Wickham Freight Lines. “We were genuinely impressed. I’m a true believer. I love the technology and I’m not a true tech person whatsoever. You can just see that it’s a winner … the performance, reliability and operational savings were beyond what we expected. For a business like ours, running a large fleet across the east coast, with a heavy focus on refrigerated and cold chain freight, this technology makes real commercial sense.”

Sunswap Endurance first showed their new solar reefer unit at HVIA TruckShowX in Hunter Valley this May past. It’s compelling, insultingly simple technology and I, for one, hope this customer delivery is just the first of many. Let us know what you think of these guys, in the comments.

Solar powered refrigeration truck looks like a natural combination. Cost of the solar is offset somewhat by not needing diesel tank, motor, and generator. Majority of savings probably come form not needing constant refueling (fuel + labor), or in not needing to overhaul the engine periodically.

I would be very interested in knowing how quickly the system pays for itself.

#4804. Beyond Bars and Into Being

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Midway through the 2024 film "Sing Sing," a group of men rehearses a play in a classroom at a maximum-security prison in New York (Kwedar, 2024). Some of the actors learned their craft while they were incarcerated. They are alumni of Rehabilitation Through the Arts (RTA), the theater program the film portrays, and on screen they play versions of themselves.

RTA makes a striking claim about what happens after its participants go home: only around 5% return to prison (ABC7 New York, 2022). Nationally, 27% of people released from prison are reincarcerated within three years, down from 35% for those released in 2008 (Council of State Governments [CSG] Justice Center, 2024). The national figure is moving in the right direction. RTA’s figure suggests the arts may be reaching people in ways standard rehabilitation misses.

One possibility is that creative engagement addresses barriers conventional re-entry programs tend to overlook: trauma, a disrupted sense of self, and strained emotional capacity. The idea is promising, and the research behind it is still young.

The past two decades have brought new investment in re-entry, including the Second Chance Act of 2008, which funded education, mental health care, and substance use treatment for people leaving prison (CSG Justice Center, 2024). Attending to these needs is valuable; however, far less attention goes to what years inside do to a person’s mind and body. “The legal system, and incarceration more specifically, produces a legacy of intergenerational trauma and health harms,” says Dr. Rebecca Fix, an Assistant Professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “Instead of addressing the traumatic circumstances that led many to incarceration, prisons exacerbate those harms.”

In a study of about 4,000 incarcerated men, 44.7% reported physical trauma in childhood (Wolff & Shi, 2012). Current rates of post-traumatic stress disorder are roughly five times more common among men in prison than in the general population, and about eight times more common among women (Baranyi et al., 2018). Experiences in prison typically perpetuate this trauma and distress. Victimization, solitary confinement, and coercion experienced in prison are each associated with PTSD (Piper & Berle, 2019). Among people released after long sentences, researchers have identified a lasting cluster of symptoms that includes chronic distrust, difficulty making decisions, and trouble sustaining relationships (Liem & Kunst, 2013). Poet Reginald Dwayne Betts was incarcerated at 16 and spent 14 months in solitary confinement. His collection Felon traces how that time follows a person long after release (Betts, 2019). These are the very capacities people need to rebuild their lives at home, work, and in their families, and most re-entry services do little to restore them.

Coming home after prison means building a new story about who one is, one in which a person sees themselves as capable, creative, and worthy of a future (Maruna, 2001). Creative work offers a place to start writing that story (Fleetwood, 2020). For example, Jimmy Santiago Baca (2001) entered prison unable to read and taught himself to read and write there, emerging as a poet. Shaka Senghor (2016), who spent seven of his 19 years in prison in solitary confinement, credits literature and self-examination with helping him confront his past.

Making art engages the body and the senses along with language. In one small study of adults outside prison, 45 minutes of art-making lowered levels of the stress hormone cortisol in about three-quarters of participants (Kaimal et al., 2016). In another study, dance movement therapy lowered depression scores by 72% in 12 weeks (Jeong et al., 2005).

Theater and writing give people a place to try on a new identity. On stage, someone the system calls an inmate becomes an actor, a writer, a member of an ensemble, and an audience watches that change happen. Narrative identity research links redemptive life stories to well-being (McAdams & McLean, 2013), and performance may be one way to rehearse such a story out loud (Maruna, 2001). Ashley Lucas (2020), former director of the Prison Creative Arts Project, draws on years of directing theater in prisons to describe how performance builds community and hope in settings designed to strip both away. In Baltimore, Center Stage launched a year-long theater program in 2024 with young people held at the city’s Juvenile Justice Center (Baltimore Center Stage, n.d.). Stella Adler Studio of Acting has been partnering with the Rikers Island Correctional Facility since 2014. Every week across the year, a cadre of trained artists – including teachers, writers, voice and speech experts, movement coaches and directors – visit multiple facilities to reach hundreds of inmates annually. Ensemble work asks for turn-taking, negotiation, and impulse control, too. In an evaluation of California prison arts programs, participants reported gains in emotional control, time management, and self-confidence, and disciplinary reports fell (Brewster, 2014).

An evaluation of the University of Denver Prison Arts Initiative concluded that arts programs can “invoke liberatory experiences for participants” (Littman & Sliva, 2021, as cited in Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop, n.d.), and other studies report fewer depressive symptoms and a greater sense of self-respect and purpose among participants (Minnesota Prison Writing Workshop, n.d.).

While peer-reviewed research conducted in carceral systems is thin, though growing, a meta-analysis of arts therapies in forensic settings, including 11 randomized or controlled trials, found improvements in psychiatric symptoms and in social and psychological functioning (Abbing et al., 2023). In a randomized trial with 200 men in a Chinese prison, group music therapy reduced anxiety and depression and raised self-esteem (Chen et al., 2016).

The punitive model assumes that people choose crime and that harsher consequences will deter them. Research offers little support for that assumption: compared with non-custodial sentences, imprisonment has a null or slightly criminogenic effect on reoffending (Nagin et al., 2009). Scholars and organizers including Angela Y. Davis (2003), Ruth Wilson Gilmore (2022), and Mariame Kaba (2021) call for moving resources away from prisons and toward the people and institutions that help communities thrive.

The arts are one of those investments. “Alternatives to incarceration, including restorative and transformative approaches, ask what people and communities need to heal,” Fix explains. “For many, creative expression is part of that answer, as an alternative to the traumatic carceral environment, though arts programming within prisons can also offer meaningful support where alternatives don't yet exist.” They give people a structured, safe outlet for processing difficult experiences, room to rehearse a new identity, and a way to contribute something others value. The arts also help people who have been incarcerated speak for themselves. Ear Hustle, a podcast about life inside created at San Quentin State Prison by Earlonne Woods, who was then incarcerated there, and artist Nigel Poor, reached a national audience and was a 2020 Pulitzer Prize finalist (The Pulitzer Prizes, 2020).

The arts can be a powerful tool to support the social and emotional health of incarcerated individuals. For the men who learned to act at Sing Sing and then played themselves on screen, creative work was part of how they rebuilt their lives. Far more people leaving prison deserve the same chance.

Maya Lakshman, MPH, is a doctoral candidate at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, where she uses neuroimaging, geospatial, and qualitative methods to understand the impacts of structural and interpersonal violence on development and mental health across the lifespan. She is a writer, educator, and researcher with an interest in translating evidence into equitable, justice-centered public health policy.

#4802. Increasing Ozempic Dose Linked to Lower Heart Risk Than Switching to Mounjaro

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Increasing the dose of Ozempic rather than switching to Mounjaro may be associated with a lower risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), according to a 2026 insurance claims analysis presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting 2026 in Milan, Italy.

GLP-1 medications like semaglutide (Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro) have reshaped care for people with type 2 diabetes, but recent real-world evidence suggests these drugs may not offer identical heart protection.

It is important to keep in mind that this was a retrospective, observational study that showed an association, not causation.

More research is needed to fully compare the cardiovascular benefits of semaglutide versus tirzepatide.

The COMPETE SWITCH Cardiovascular (CV) analysis used Komodo Health’s Healthcare Map, a large US healthcare claims database with linked laboratory results, to examine real-world data from 636,525 adults with type 2 diabetes.

The analysis focused on 185,705 people who increased their semaglutide dose and 23,104 who switched to tirzepatide.

All participants included in the analysis were already receiving 1 mg of semaglutide (Ozempic) weekly.

The researchers found that people who increased their Ozempic dose to 2 mg had a 6% lower risk of MACE — including all-cause death, myocardial infarction (heart attack), and stroke — compared with those who switched to Mounjaro at doses up to 15 mg.

“This is an interesting study, but the findings may partly reflect medication adherence. When patients switch medications, it can take time to adjust the dose and find the right treatment level, which may temporarily affect how well their condition is controlled,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

He also noted that the study did not determine what might explain the difference in cardiovascular risk.

“It may be related to a combination of weight loss and direct effects on hormones involved in metabolism and appetite regulation,” Ali said.

Semaglutide and tirzepatide are both GLP-1 medications. Ozempic (semaglutide) and Mounjaro (tirzepatide) are approved to help manage type 2 diabetes, while each medication also has a different brand approved for weight loss.

The semaglutide approved for weight loss in the U.S. is sold as Wegovy, and the tirzepatide approved for weight loss is sold as Zepbound.

“Semaglutide and tirzepatide work in a similar way. While semaglutide is a direct GLP-1 receptor agonist, tirzepatide is a dual agonist of both the GIP and GLP-1 receptors,” Amit Blumfield, MD, with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

“Because they work through somewhat different pathways, they can have different effects in individual patients,” added Ali.

While both semaglutide (Ozemipc) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro) work in similar ways, you may find that you tolerate one better than the other.

Ali noted that you should discuss any potential benefits and drawbacks with your healthcare professional.

“I would only recommend switching medications if there is an issue with tolerance of one or the other. If one medication is well-tolerated at increasingly higher doses and is effective in the desired weight-loss and blood sugar management, I wouldn’t necessarily switch,” added Blumfield.

These side effects are generally mild and may lessen over time. However, if side effects become difficult to tolerate, you should speak with your healthcare professional.

“GLP-1 medications can be highly effective for managing diabetes and promoting weight loss, but there is no one-size-fits-all treatment. The best medication depends on an individual’s health needs, goals, response to treatment, and potential side effects,” said Ali.

#4801. XCMG debuts new, fully autonomous electric terminal tractor [video]

The new XCMG SDA411 concept terminal truck is fully electric, has no cabin, and an L4 autonomous tech stack that’s purpose-built for unmanned logistics – and, if XCMG get their way, it looks like the future of drayage truck operations.

Whether you call them terminal trucks, yard dogs, or anything else, these heavy-duty trucks do work that’s ideally suited to electrification. It’s all low-speed, high-torque, short distance, precision operation, all the time. And the quiet, vibration-free, instant power operation of electric drive is in its element.

Chinese equipment brand XCMG gets it, and they’re taking the electric terminal truck concept a step further with the debut of an all-new, cab-less design that’s 100% autonomous.

“With no cab and an L4 autonomous driving system, the platform is purpose-built for unmanned logistics,” said XCMG, on LinkedIn. “Its 360° perception system enables autonomous navigation, obstacle avoidance, task execution and parking, supporting continuous mixed-traffic operations in demanding environments.”

That same post included a video showing the SDA411 make its way around XCMG’s campus, making some emergency stops, and pulling up to a charger for a human attendant to plug it in (I guess they haven’t heard about Fortescue’s trick with the KUKA welding robot, yet). You can check out the post for yourself, below.

As for the autonomous aspect, while I generally side with labor and humanity over management and technology, there’s some truth to the industry claims that young people don’t want to drive trucks anymore, even with the promise of six-figure salaries.

Combine that with an aging workforce and not enough new talent entering the field, and virtually every industrial sector is struggling with a serious operator shortage. Autonomous equipment like the SDA411 could help address that shortage, keeping goods moving even when there aren’t enough drivers to go around. And rather than simply replacing workers, the technology could let experienced operators oversee multiple vehicles, take on supervisory roles and stay in the industry longer, while making these jobs accessible to people who might not otherwise be able to do them.

It doesn’t have to be autonomous because it’s electric it only needs to be powered by electric motors not gas to be better in every way.

If XCMG get their way, we’ll get to see how that all plays out somewhat sooner than later. In the meantime, we’ll have to settle for hearing what you think about the SDA411 and how it could impact brands like Kalmar and Orange EV in the comments.

#4800. This lava planet shouldn’t have an atmosphere—but it does

Published Oct 27, 2026 11:32 AM EDT

The exoplanet TOI-561 b is fascinating to observe from 280 light-years away—but it’s not a place anyone would want to visit. Not only is it blanketed by an ocean of molten lava, but TOI-561 b is constantly bombarded by destructive radiation from its host star. The planet endures so much stellar energy that astronomers have long assumed its atmosphere evaporated eons ago.

However, new observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) contradict those initial conceptions. After examining TOI-561 b for 37 hours—almost four complete orbits—researchers now believe the planetary lava lamp actually features a thick atmospheric shell. The surprising evidence recently detailed in The Astronomical Journal isn’t what scientists assumed from a planet under such stellar duress.

“Our discovery challenges current theories,” said study co-author and University of Birmingham astronomer Anjali Piette. “We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.”

Like Earth’s moon, TOI-561 b is tidally locked, which means its rotation coincides almost exactly with the time it takes to orbit its star. This ensures one side of the planet constantly experiences daylight, while its other half is always enveloped in darkness. JWST’s extensive observation window allowed Piette and her colleagues to study TOI-561 b’s phase curve—how its brightness and heat shift during its orbit. However, the results didn’t make sense. The planet’s dayside was cooler than it should be, while the nightside didn’t account for the temperature difference.

“[We] revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side,” explained University of Waterloo astrophysicist and study co-author Lisa Dang. “Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere.”

It’s likely not a thin layer of clouds, either.

“The evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today,” added Piette.

Computer simulations of TOI-561 b’s climate indicate that its atmosphere is possibly composed of silicate minerals like silicon dioxide and magnesium silicate. If true, these would hypothetically reflect much of the harmful stellar radiation away from the planet’s surface. Regardless, the discovery creates more questions than it answers. It could be that TOI-561 b simply began with a huge quantity of gas. Another theory contends that the planet-wide molten ocean functions like a single, gigantic volcano that continually supplies gas into its atmosphere.

Armed with the new data, astronomers next hope to determine whether TOI-561 b resembles a hotter version of Venus that reflects about three-quarters of starlight, or if it operates like a superpowered iteration of Jupiter’s volcanic moon, Io. Either way, JWST will be called into service once again.“Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years,” said Dang.

#4798. Oral GLP-1 Orforglipron (Foundayo) Achieves Weight Loss for Women of All Ages

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new GLP-1 pill called orforglipron (Foundayo) has been shown to help women lose weight, regardless of menopausal status, according to new research.

A group of researchers, including senior author Hunter Thomas Hoffman, PharmD, a clinical research scientist affiliated with the drug’s manufacturer, Eli Lilly, analyzed data from two prior trials, ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2, to arrive at this conclusion.

These studies reveal that this medication works equally well for women who have not yet gone through menopause, those who are currently experiencing it, and those who are postmenopausal.

The findings were presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD), held in Milan, Italy, from September 28 to October 2.

This is important because menopause often causes weight gain due to lower estrogen levels, making weight loss more difficult for many women.

Orforglipron offers a promising new option for managing weight in women with obesity or overweight, especially those with type 2 diabetes.

In April of this year, Eli Lilly’s Foundayo received FDA approval as a weight-loss drug, making it the second GLP-1 pill for weight loss to enter the U.S. market after Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy.

The ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 studies involved women who were either obese or overweight and who had at least one medical condition related to their weight.

Obesity was defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, and overweight as a BMI of 27 or higher.

The participants were divided into groups based on their menopausal status: premenopausal (before menopause), perimenopausal (during the menopause transition), and postmenopausal (after menopause).

Each group included between 142 and 225 females who either received orforglipron or placebo, an inactive pill with none of the drug in it.

The ATTAIN-1 study focused on people who were overweight or obese but did not have diabetes. ATTAIN-2 included participants who had both overweight or obesity and type 2 diabetes.

The purpose of analyzing these two groups separately was to understand how orforglipron works in people with different health conditions.

The researchers measured several outcomes over a period of 72 weeks. They examined changes in body weight, waist circumference (the distance around the waist), and the waist-to-height ratio, a measure used to assess body fat distribution.

They also tracked how many women reached specific weight loss goals, such as losing at least 5%, 10%, 15%, or 20% of their body weight, compared to those who took the inactive pill.

By studying these factors, the researchers were able to determine not only whether orforglipron helped women lose weight but also how much weight loss was achieved and how it affected their body shape.

The results showed that women who took orforglipron experienced significant weight loss regardless of their menopausal status.

In the ATTAIN-1 and ATTAIN-2 studies, premenopausal, perimenopausal, and postmenopausal women all lost an average of up to 14% of their body weight.

This means that the medication was effective for women at different life stages, including those experiencing menopause, when weight gain is often a challenge.

In addition to losing body weight, women in the orforglipron groups also saw meaningful reductions in waist circumference. Waist measurements decreased by up to 12.5 centimeters (about 5 inches) across all menopausal groups in both studies.

This reduction is important because greater visceral fat is associated with higher risks of heart disease and diabetes.

The waist-to-height ratio also improved for many women taking orforglipron. More participants treated with the medication moved into lower waist-to-height ratio categories than those who took the placebo.

This indicates a healthier distribution of body fat and suggests a lower risk of heart disease.

When looking at the number of women who reached specific weight loss milestones, orforglipron performed much better than the placebo. Up to 83% of women on orforglipron lost at least 5% of their body weight, while 30% of women on placebo reached that same level of weight loss.

Losing 5% or more of body weight is often considered clinically meaningful, as it can lead to improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels.

Overall, these findings suggest that orforglipron is a promising new medication for weight management in women with obesity or overweight, including those who also have type 2 diabetes.

This can be especially helpful for those navigating the challenges of menopause while trying to manage their weight.

James J. Chao, MD, FACS, Chief Medical Officer and co-founder of VedaNu Wellness, wasn’t involved in the research, but said the significance of these findings for postmenopausal women.

“The 14% is what’s grabbing headlines,” he told Healthline, “but up to 12.5 cm from the waistline is what I’m interested in.”

According to Chao, as females enter postmenopause, they tend to store more fat around their midsection.

“This is the type of fat that can cause heart disease,” he said. “So a pill that can help a 38-year-old woman lose the same amount as a 62-year-old breaks that myth.”

Additionally, in contrast to most GLP-1 drugs, which are injectable, it’s a once-a-day pill. You can also take it any time, Chao explained, making it more convenient.

“No needle, no refrigerator, and up to 83% of participants lost at least 5%,” he said. “Sometimes it’s the simple things that make a difference.”

Luca Moretti, MD, a medical doctor at Sapienza University of Rome, who wasn’t involved in the studies, added that convenience isn’t the only thing to consider when deciding whether to use orforglipron.

Obesity management should begin with an individualized plan that includes nutrition, physical activity, and the management of other risk factors.

“When these measures are not sufficient, adding pharmacological treatment can be considered together with a physician,” he told Healthline.

Moretti further advised speaking with your physician about any potential side effects, your existing medical conditions, other medications you are taking, and your treatment preferences.

“So the most useful question to ask a doctor is not simply, ‘Is Foundayo more convenient?’ but rather: ‘Among the available treatments, which one offers the best balance of effectiveness, tolerability, and practicality for me?'” he said.

#4797. Navigating the Holidays When You're Estranged From Family

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

Knowing you had to cut ties with your parent to protect yourself doesn't make the holidays any easier. It's normal to miss having a family to celebrate with, feel guilty about not being together, or dread questions about why you're not seeing your parents. Even when you know you've made the right decision, the holidays can bring up feelings you thought you'd worked through.

Here's how to navigate the season in a way that protects your well-being and helps you regain some joy.

For many adult children of dysfunctional parents, holidays can be painful reminders of both your current reality and what you've lost. You may find yourself grieving the parent you're estranged from, but also the parent you always wished you'd had. It's completely natural to feel confused or upset; part of you may still long for a nurturing, loving connection, while another part knows that staying in a toxic relationship would only cause more pain.

Holidays can amplify these feelings because they're built around an idealized version of family that's never been your reality. You may feel pressure to attend gatherings that feel unsafe, or you may be flooded with painful memories when everyone around you seems to be celebrating. The goal is to learn to tolerate such feelings, knowing that they will lessen, and to treat yourself with compassion.

The first decision is whether to attend family events at all. This is always a choice, even when it doesn't feel like one. Choosing not to attend a gathering when your estranged parent will be there isn’t necessarily a sign of avoidance but of maintaining a boundary. If you do choose to attend, it should be because it genuinely serves you—and not because of guilt, obligation, or pressure from others.

Take time to weigh your options. Ask yourself: What's the emotional cost of attending? What do you hope to gain—and is it realistic? And will being there require you to compromise your boundaries or safety? (For people with abusive or toxic parents, skipping a holiday gathering may be the healthiest decision.)

Once you've made your decision, preparation can help you avoid reactive choices in an already emotional situation. Anxiety can build for days or weeks before a difficult holiday, so don't wait until the day arrives to think through your approach.

If you're not attending: Resist the pull to leave the day unstructured. A completely open day can intensify rumination and sadness. Plan something intentional that gives you something grounded to move toward.

If you're attending: Go in with a clear plan so you feel more grounded and in control.

Estrangement invites you to rethink what holidays can look like. You don't have to organize your life around traditions that cause pain; giving yourself permission to step away is progress in itself.

Think creatively about how you want to spend the holiday. Start new traditions, volunteer, or do something you genuinely enjoy but rarely make time for—a hike, a movie, or a good book. It's also completely fine to use the time to rest, reflect, practice self-care, do chores, or pursue hobbies. There are no rules: How you spend the day is completely up to you, whether that means making new meaning out of the holiday or simply getting through it in whatever way feels manageable.

Holidays can be emotionally draining, regardless of what you decide to do. In my book, Cutting Ties with Your Parents, I share these strategies for getting through the season:

Journaling is one of the most effective tools for working through complicated emotions; it slows your thinking and brings clarity. Try reflecting on questions like, What am I grieving today? What do I wish I'd received from my parents that I didn't? and What do I need right now, and how can I give it to myself?

If anxiety or distressing memories surface, try a grounding exercise, deep breathing, or a guided meditation to help interrupt the stress response.

Estrangement can’t erase the hurt you've experienced, but it can create space for healing. With each holiday you navigate, you may build more clarity about who you are, what you need, and what matters most to you. With practice, you’ll move from simply surviving the season to building traditions and relationships that feel safer, healthier, and more joyful.

#4796. Amflow launches two powerful new electric bikes, including its first SUV-style e-bike

Amflow, the electric bicycle brand that burst onto the scene with some of the most powerful and lightweight electric mountain bikes on the market, is expanding its lineup with two major releases. The company has announced global availability of its new Amflow TL Carbon, while also bringing its removable-battery Amflow PR Carbon series to the US for the first time.

Both models are powered by the latest Avinox mid-drive motor systems, which have quickly earned a reputation for delivering impressive power in surprisingly compact packages.

The biggest departure from Amflow’s roots is the new TL Carbon, which takes the company’s high-performance mountain biking DNA and applies it to a more versatile SUV-style electric bike. While less common in the US (ironically), SUV-style e-bikes are essentially a hybrid electric bicycle designed to act as an all-in-one, “do-it-all” vehicle combining the rugged build and off-road capability of an electric mountain bike with the practical, everyday utility of a city or trekking bike.

Rather than focusing exclusively on technical trails and aggressive mountain biking, the TL Carbon is designed to handle everything from daily commuting to touring and off-road adventures. And with Avinox’s RS800 battery featuring 800Wh of capacity, it’s got plenty of energy on board for diverse adventures.

The full-suspension bike uses the Avinox M2 motor, delivering up to 125 Nm of torque, which should provide more than enough grunt for steep climbs, heavy loads, and just about anything else riders can throw at it.

Avinox e-bike drive systems are known for many things, but chief among them is the extremely high power and torque they offer, eclipsing most other mid-drive motor systems on the market.

Despite that power and versatility, the TL Carbon weighs as little as 22.6 kg (49.8 lb). It also boasts an impressive maximum total weight capacity of 200 kg (441 lb), including the bike itself, rider, and cargo carried on its front and rear racks.

That’s a compelling combination for riders who want the performance of a premium electric mountain bike but need something practical enough to replace a car for everyday trips.

And perhaps most surprisingly, the price isn’t completely outrageous. The Amflow TL Carbon starts at $3,899 in the US and €3,499 in Germany, positioning it competitively against premium European trekking and SUV-style e-bikes.

Meanwhile, American riders are finally getting access to the Amflow PR Carbon series, which had previously launched in other markets.

Unlike Amflow’s earlier electric mountain bikes, the PR series features a removable battery, addressing one of the biggest practical complaints about high-performance eMTBs with integrated batteries.

The new 800 Wh battery weighs just 4 kg (8.8 lb) and can be removed for convenient indoor charging or swapped for a fresh battery to extend a ride. That’s especially useful for riders who don’t have a convenient charging outlet near their bike storage area.

Amflow claims up to 158 km (98 miles) of range under ideal conditions, though that’s based on relatively gentle riding on flat pavement in Eco mode. Riders tackling technical trails with high assistance levels should expect considerably less. But any way you slice it, 800 Wh is a huge battery for eMTBs and should deliver plenty of range under most conditions.

The standard PR Carbon uses the Avinox M2 motor with up to 125 Nm of torque, while the higher-end PR Carbon Pro upgrades to the more powerful Avinox M2S motor, producing up to 150 Nm of torque.

In the US, the PR Carbon starts at $4,999, while the PR Carbon Pro commands $6,799. European pricing starts at €4,499 and €5,899, respectively, based on German pricing.

All three bikes are available beginning today through ⁠Amflow’s official website and its network of authorized dealers. In the US, both models generally arrive as Class 1 e-bikes (no throttle) with a top speed of 20 mph (32 km/h), though Amflow models can typically be unlocked to Class 3 performance with a top speed of 28 mph (45 km/h).

Amflow has been one of the more interesting brands to watch in the premium e-bike space, largely because of how aggressively it has pushed the boundaries of motor performance and bike weight.

But these latest releases show that the company is thinking beyond simply building increasingly powerful electric mountain bikes.

The TL Carbon is particularly interesting to me because it brings that impressive Avinox performance to a more practical platform. As someone who spends a minority of my riding time in the dirt, Amflow suddenly looks a lot more interesting to me, personally. Not everyone needs a dedicated eMTB, but plenty of riders would appreciate a lightweight, powerful, well-equipped electric bike that can handle both weekday commuting and weekend adventures.

And the PR Carbon’s removable battery is a welcome development, especially as the industry continues to recognize that convenience and serviceability matter just as much as outright performance.

With the Avinox ecosystem continuing to expand across more bike brands and categories, Amflow is also facing increasing competition from other manufacturers using the same impressive motors. That makes it all the more important for the brand to differentiate itself through thoughtful bike design, not just headline-grabbing power figures.

#4795. How to avoid the iPhone’s notorious ‘silent alarm’ bug

Updated Oct 27, 2026 12:54 PM EDT

You might’ve seen recent reports of users complaining that they’ve slept through alarms set on their iPhones–or even encountered it yourself. But it’s not a new bug. The silent iPhone alarm issue has plagued users for at least a couple of years, and still keeps affecting people (even though Apple has previously promised to fix it).

The bug causes alarms to go off, but silently—there’s no audible ring, and no vibration. That’s not ideal if you need to get up for work, a flight, or anything else you have to do. So what exactly is going on? Here’s what we know about the so-called silent alarm bug on the iPhone and what you can do about it.

You can rule out Silent mode and Do Not Disturb. According to Apple, your alarm still sounds when either one is turned on.

If you set an alarm, it’s important that it actually alerts you at the right time. But these silent alarms that users have been noticing on their iPhones don’t make any sound and don’t trigger any vibrations. They do appear on screen as normal, but they’re completely silent.

As for what’s causing it, no one seems certain. Back in 2024, Apple said it was fixing the issue, without going into much detail about what was behind it—but users are finding that it’s still happening. Sometimes it seems that a particular iOS version will patch the problem, only for it to show up again in a subsequent version.

Given that it’s been happening for a long time, and affecting a substantial number of users (but not everyone), it’s possible that there are multiple causes. Apple hasn’t explained what’s behind it, but its alarm support page lists troubleshooting steps, and there are other things you can do to minimize the likelihood of silent alarms.

First, make sure your alarms are set as intended from the Alarms tab of the Clock app. Tap on an alarm and you can check the Sound option to see the noise it triggers and the Repeat option to check the frequency—it may be that your alarm is set to go off some days and not others. If a specific alarm isn’t ringing, try deleting it and creating it again.

You can get to the audio settings for your iPhone by opening up Settings, then choosing Sounds & Haptics. Look at the volume slider under Ringtone and Alerts to make sure it’s high enough. You might also want to turn off Change with Buttons to make sure you’re not adjusting the alert volume accidentally. Alarms aren’t affected by the Silent Mode toggle or the Ring/Silent switch, so you don’t need to change either one.

Connected headphones aren’t likely to be the culprit, either. Apple says that if wired or wireless headphones are connected, your alarm plays through the iPhone’s built-in speakers as well as the headphones.

Some users have found they can overcome the silent alarm bug by turning off the Attention-Aware Features toggle switch, which you’ll find under Face ID & Passcode in Settings. This changes certain iPhone behaviors, including the level of alarm sounds, if it thinks you’re looking at the screen. It could explain certain silent alarms—though it should only ever lower the alarm volume level, not mute it completely.

If your alarm makes a sound but doesn’t vibrate, check whether your iPhone was in StandBy, the full-screen clock view that appears when the phone is charging on its side. Apple turns off alarm haptics in StandBy, so you’ll only get the sound.

Do Not Disturb and any other modes you’ve set up in Focus in Settings don’t silence alarms either. They control notifications from apps and people, so they’re unlikely to be behind the problem.

Apple also warns that manually changing the time on your iPhone (a trick some people use to skip game timers) can affect alarms. Leave Set Automatically turned on under General > Date & Time in Settings.

Finally, be sure to keep your iPhone up to date with the latest version of iOS. While it seems as though this bug is persisting in the latest software releases, hopefully at some point Apple will squash it for good, and when that happens you’re going to want to get the update as soon as possible.

Not every missed alarm is the silent bug. When iOS 26 launched, Apple redesigned the alarm screen with large Stop and Snooze buttons sitting close together, which made it easy to stop an alarm when you meant to snooze it. In iOS 26.1, Apple replaced the Stop button with a Slide to stop gesture, while Snooze is still a single tap.

If your alarms are ringing but you keep switching them off half-asleep, open Settings and go to Accessibility > Touch. If Prefer Single-Touch Actions is turned on, your iPhone swaps the slider back for a one-tap Stop button. Turn it off to get the slider back. The setting changes other sliders across iOS too, not just alarms.

Something else you can do to try and avoid silent alarms is to install a third-party alarm app, and there are lots to choose from. Alarmy actually prides itself on the loudness of its alarm alerts, so you should have no problems waking up. You can get some extra premium features and remove the ads by paying $4.99 a month, but the basic functionality is free.

Sleep Cycle is another app worth considering. Not only will it wake you up, it also has a smart alarm feature that aims to rouse you at the most beneficial time in your sleep cycle (within a preset window). It’ll track your sleep too—there’s a lot to it. You get the basics for free, with a pile of premium features (including weather reports and more sleep stats) available for a $2.99-per-month subscription.

Or you can invest in a smart alarm clock. Or just an old-fashioned alarm clock with the big red numbers and real buttons.

#4794. All aboard! Massachusetts is getting 10 new electric transit trains

The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) board of directors voted unanimously Thursday to approve the purchase of a new generation of battery-powered public transit trains – and they can’t arrive soon enough.

“(MBTA) has, obviously, an immediate need for locomotives,” explains William Wolfgang, the MBTA’s senior director of vehicle engineering. The new machines will replace the oldest locomotives in the MBTA fleet, GP40s built more than 50 years ago and F40s that are well over 30 years old. In a presentation to the MTBA board, MTBA said 13 of the GP40s have, “exceeded their useful life,” while the F40s will reach the end of their life between 2029 and 2035.

The MBTA will put in an order for 20 Siemens-built “Charger” locomotives; 10 Tier 4 diesel-powered hybrid electric units and 10 dual-mode battery/catenary electric units – and, beyond trackside power for charging the batteries, there are other challenges presented by going electric, most notably using existing cab cars to control the battery-electric units. “We’re going to have to work with railroad operations, engineering, and the Brotherhood of [Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen] to try and determine the best way to handle that,” adds Wolfgang. “That will be an upcoming change order once we get into the design review process.”

The total bill comes out to $310.4 million. A combination of state and federal funding will pay for the order, including a recent $200 million transfer from the Massachusetts Department of Transportation.

The contract includes an option for additional locomotives, although details were not discussed during the meeting. Delivery of the new Siemens Charger trains is set to begin in 2029, with all 20 set to be in service by the end of 2030. Siemens has delivered 440 Charger model hybrid- and battery-electric locomotives globally at the time of this writing.

#4793. Silly bear cub wins award for being terrible at hide-and-seek

Published Oct 27, 2026 12:57 PM EDT

Baby bears need to learn a lot during their first few summers—how to catch salmon, how to swim, how to climb trees, the importance of avoiding porcupine quills, etc. For one cub in Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, learning how to play hide & seek was added to that growing list of skills.

The United States Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest have awarded the official 2026 Worst at Hide-and-Seek Award to a baby bear who needs a bit more practice at this game. The baby bear belongs to Osso, who won the 2026 Mama Bear Award for her prowess.

“It [the cub] stole our Rangers’ hearts,” the team writes. “It looked like it wanted to play hide and seek but couldn’t fully grasp the concept. Our Rangers were glad the cub was bad at the game, because it meant they saw it more.”

Osso had three cubs this season. However, Rangers only spotted her with two cubs in August and believe that one died. Black bear cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent depending on the location.

Tongass is the nation’s largest national forest and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, which is home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 known bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their counterparts further to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return here every summer to eat salmon and teach their young how to fish and survive. And also like the bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear and explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4792. The Loneliness Trap

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 3, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

With unyielding inflation, economic uncertainty, and geopolitical friction sending collective anxiety levels higher and higher, many of us now consider genuine contentment an unaffordable luxury. Yet many decades of history serve as reminders that even amidst tremendous upheaval, human joy has never depended on what you can buy or external calm.

In this challenging environment, most of us want what we’ve always wanted: to be genuinely happy. Yet we are not willing to do what it takes to become happy.

A study from almost a century ago of the residents of the Northern English town of Bolton shows us the severe effects of not carving out time for our loved ones, a decision that most of us make every day. In the year my father was born, just over 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) to the east in Hungary, 1938—and then again in 2014—the residents of Bolton were asked what made them happy.

The most common ingredients of happiness among responses spanning 78 years were economic security and personal relationships, which were often tied together. Little mention was made of external events.

Joseph Roberts, a miner, despite answering the survey in 1938 when the threat of Hitler loomed large—the Nazi leader had already occupied Austria and parts of what was then Czechoslovakia—shared that what made him happy was returning from a day of hard work and spending time with his family.

“I see my kiddies and wife I am happy,” shared the miner. “When I am washed and romp with my kiddies, and when it is weekend and I tip up my humble wage and share with my wife in doling it out and we find we can manage another week we are happy. I am in regular work although it is hard and dangerous but I am happy because I have a contented mind.”

I am guessing you would agree that happiness is a seed you must grow in your life. Yet what most people do not understand is that you can’t grow your happiness alone; you can only do so with the help of others.

Since you cannot grow your happiness alone, it must also be true that happiness is a seed that grows in the gardens of others. How does this work?

We all seek happiness yet find it elusive. The reason is that most of us do not realize that one of the best ways to experience happiness is to help others experience it.

Plato understood this well. “Caring for the happiness of others,” observed the Greek philosopher over 2,500 years ago, “we find our own.”

Research also bears this out. Not only do people feel even more appreciated, happy, and connected to us than we expect them to when we give to them, but we also counterintuitively often benefit, as psychologists Sonja Lyubomirsky and Harry Reis note in their book How to Feel Loved, even more than they do.

I was reminded of this truth last month, when I spent nine days in a small town in rural Kenya where I had lived and worked as a Peace Corps volunteer 35 years earlier. Facilitating a pro bono leadership conference for rural primary and secondary school leaders and supporting five Kenyan women educators in teaching a women’s empowerment program for single mothers in one of Kenya’s most impoverished regions, I was struck by how happy I felt connecting with the people around me.

Returning to my comparatively more hermetic life of writing, researching, and teaching in Rome has been a jolt to my system; yet the memories remain and bring peace. In the end, I am like everyone else I’ve ever met in the world: traveling on an eternal search for connection and meaning.

Following the Italian way of expressing love, when you tell the other person “Ti voglio bene” (which means “I wish for your happiness”), you offer them the seed of happiness to plant in their own garden. You give them your support to grow in the way they desire, toward their own goals and values, or “to become,” as the former president of the American Psychological Association and the father of client-centered therapy, Carl Rogers, once wrote.

If the seed flourishes and becomes the flower of happiness, the other person may or may not bring you this flower one day. Sound risky? It may be; yet it’s the only way you will ever have the experience of seeing this flower in full bloom.

In other words, interconnectedness is the only path that will enable you to experience and sustain happiness throughout your life.

“Sounds good, Mr. Idealistic Author,” you may be thinking. “But how do I make daily decisions that will bring this interconnectedness into my life?”

If you want a more interconnected life, you will first have to ask yourself some tough questions about your daily decisions, right down to whether you should spend your time today ordering another gadget on Amazon or going hiking with a friend. Let’s consider this choice.

What do you think will bring you more happiness—an Amazon delivery or going on a hike with a friend? A study by Amit Kumar of the University of Texas has found that once you have a base level of financial resources, experiences rather than objects are the drivers of happiness.

Why? Experiences (“doing” something such as going to a meditation retreat or on a bicycle ride or to a restaurant or a concert) are more often shared, while objects (“owning” something such as a new shirt or book) are most often enjoyed alone.

In the end, the love we’ve shared with others is all we take with us. “All that we love deeply,” Helen Keller sagely observed, “becomes a part of us.” This is why experiences, which facilitate the sharing of love, produce much more long-term happiness than objects.

How, then, can you usher more happiness back into your life? Prioritize doing activities you enjoy in person with people you care about rather than buying objects to enjoy by your lonesome.

Just as you pursue objects to purchase and yet Prime shipping does not drop happiness at your doorstep, you also pursue social information about the people in your social network. As I write in my book Screened In, this search—like buying objects—does not bring the social connection that is the purveyor of genuine happiness into your life.

In sum, then, stop texting and call, go out with, see, visit, meet—in short, spend time with other, values-congruent people as often as you can.

In other words: Just. Connect. In person. In real time.

Spend time with the people you love, or could love if you were to get to know them better. Then happiness will cease to be a distant stranger and will become a part of your life again.
